Title: 'Peace' in the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus: Good Practices and Recommendations
Abstract:
The document, co-financed by the EU, highlights the integration of peace within the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus, showcasing ten case studies from diverse geographical regions. It addresses challenges and progress since the EU's 2016 commitment to link its humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding efforts.

The countries involved are Iraq, Myanmar, Nigeria, South Sudan, Burundi, Liberia, Somalia, Lebanon, East Africa, and the Sahel region. Recommendations emphasize strategic implementation of the HDP nexus, acknowledging peacebuilding as a full component, and promoting people-centered, conflict-sensitive approaches.

The document advocates for systemic integrations, coordination, and complementarity among stakeholders like CSOs and governments. Flexible, long-term funding and the incorporation of climate change considerations underscore the strategic direction in fostering peace and resilience against violence and instability, aiming for sustainable development outcomes.

Title: 'Peace' in the Humanitarian-Development-Peacebuilding Nexus Learning and Practice Note
Abstract:
The document, produced by the Network for Conflict Prevention and Peacebuilding, provides insights and practical guidance on integrating 'peace' within the Humanitarian-Development-Peacebuilding (HDP) nexus. Focusing on Danish civil society organizations and their international partners, it examines bottom-up peacebuilding approaches which emphasize community-driven conflict resolution, long-term engagement, trust-building, and conflict sensitivity. 

The potential benefits include enhancing humanitarian and development interventions by fostering social cohesion and reducing conflict by empowering local actors and utilizing local resources for peace. Significant barriers are identified, such as short-term funding, siloed funding streams, and misunderstandings around peacebuilding. 

Promising practices include people-centered approaches and strong local partnerships to enable comprehensive context analysis and adaptability. The note serves as a resource for practitioners to operationalize these practices across the HDP nexus globally.

Title: 2024 Report on Financing Flows and Food Crises
Abstract:
Annual report (FAO/Global Network Against Food Crises, 2024) providing a comprehensive analysis of humanitarian and development financing flows to food sectors in food crisis countries — the fourth edition of the series and a companion publication to the Global Report on Food Crises (GRFC).

Drawing on data from OECD DAC, IATI, OCHA's Financial Tracking Service and other sources, it maps where funding is going, identifies underfunded and forgotten crises, and tracks trends since 2016. Key findings for 2023: humanitarian assistance to food sectors fell 30% from the 2022 peak; development financing remains overwhelmingly low, with only 3% of global development funding reaching food sectors in crisis contexts; and protracted food crises attract the least development investment despite the greatest structural need.

The report argues that financing continues to address symptoms rather than drivers of food crises, and calls for a rebalancing toward agricultural investment, integrated sequencing of food assistance and nutrition with emergency agriculture, and greater use of evidence in funding decisions. Includes country and regional breakdowns, analysis of the ten largest recipients, sectoral breakdowns, and an overview of GNAFC partner tools for tracking food crisis financing.

Title: A Caritas Europa approach to the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract: This Caritas Europa position paper presents the organisation's policy positions on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace nexus and its implementation. Building on Caritas Europa's 2024 approach paper to the nexus, this document articulates more specific positions on key policy questions — including the role of faith-based organisations in the nexus, the risks of securitisation, the importance of maintaining humanitarian principles, and recommendations for the EU's nexus policy. It contributes to civil society advocacy for a more principled, effective, and locally-grounded approach to the nexus in EU external action.

Title: A Caritas Europa approach to the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:
The Caritas Europa policy paper explores the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (Triple Nexus) as a transformative approach to address complex global challenges by integrating development, humanitarian, and peace efforts. Emphasizing local leadership, climate change, and fragile contexts, the paper presents Caritas\'s approach as rooted in Catholic Social Teachings, advocating for the holistic well-being of communities. It highlights the importance of overcoming traditional silos through bottom-up approaches, coordinated programming, and comprehensive stakeholder engagement.

The paper underscores challenges in operationalizing the Nexus, like politicization of aid and the need for clear donor policies, while proposing strategic recommendations for effective implementation. It calls for systematic funding models, strategic cooperation with local civil societies, and flexible, predictable financing to foster inclusive, sustainable development.

Case studies from Ukraine, Colombia, Zambia, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Uganda, and Myanmar highlight the practical application of Nexus principles, showcasing efforts in peacebuilding, climate adaptation, and strengthening local capacities. Ultimately, Caritas Europa advocates for further developing internal strategies, reflecting on the peace and climate components of the Nexus, and increasing collaboration among donors and organizations for a better integrated response to crises.

Title: A collection of best practices and recommendations for effective nexus delivery
Abstract:
This document, resulting from Alliance2015's multi-country learning exercise, articulates best practices and recommendations for HDP Nexus programming. It emphasizes the importance of multisector partnerships, community-led interventions, flexible, long-term adaptation, and diversified funding sources to address humanitarian, development, and peace challenges effectively. Case studies from Kenya, Ethiopia, Niger, Malawi, Lebanon, Nepal, and Burkina Faso illustrate successful Nexus approaches in diverse contexts.

Key recommendations highlight contextualized program design, integration of Nexus components throughout the project lifecycle, adaptive management, and inclusive partnerships. The document advocates for strengthening the peace pillar in Nexus initiatives while fostering continual learning and cooperation among Alliance2015 partners to advance these strategies.

Case studies in the annex provide detailed insights into specific country projects that successfully implement Nexus principles.

Title: A Critical Analysis of the War and the Triple Nexus in Northern Mozambique
Abstract:
Chapter 12 of the Global Policy triple nexus e-book series, this contribution examines triple nexus dynamics in Cabo Delgado, Northern Mozambique — an under-studied context where armed conflict intersects with major extractive industry projects and complex international interests.

The author identifies three distinct conceptions of the triple nexus operating simultaneously: a securitised/militarised nexus driven by counterinsurgency agendas of the Mozambican government and its military partners; a liberal institutional nexus promoted by the UN and IOM through coordination frameworks and localisation rhetoric; and an emerging emancipatory nexus rooted in local civil society and community-led resilience.

The piece argues that without addressing the dominance of security and economic interests, nexus approaches risk serving agendas other than human security, offering an important critical lens for nexus practitioners working in resource-rich fragile contexts.

Title: A Framework for Fragility
Abstract: Working paper developing a quantitative framework for measuring and characterising state fragility, drawing on cross-country data to propose operational definitions and indicators across multiple dimensions of fragility. Provides a rigorous analytical tool for understanding which countries face the structural conditions — weak governance, conflict risk, limited institutional capacity — that make nexus approaches both most relevant and most challenging to implement. Contributes to the conceptual and analytical foundations linking fragility measurement to decisions about how donors and multilateral institutions prioritise, sequence and adapt their engagement across the humanitarian, development and peace pillars.

Title: A guide to market-based livelihood interventions for refugees
Abstract:
This report, published by the International Labour Organization (ILO), outlines a framework for market-based livelihood interventions aimed at supporting refugees.

The report emphasizes the need for a more integrated approach that combines traditional livelihood methods with market system strategies. This involves empowering refugees with the necessary skills (push factors) and aligning market systems to provide opportunities (pull factors) for refugees, while promoting economic inclusion beneficial to both refugees and host communities.

The report considers the legal, social, and economic circumstances governing refugee access to labor markets and provides methodologies for evaluating market systems, targeting interventions, and developing sustainable livelihood strategies. Specific country examples, such as assessments conducted in Costa Rica, Egypt, and South Africa, illustrate the application of these methodologies to various contexts. Successful interventions focus on applying market analyses to identify opportunities for sustainable livelihoods, thus fostering resilience and economic growth among refugees and their host communities.

Title: A Learning Journey on the Triple Nexus: SDC Synthesis Report
Abstract:
This Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) synthesis report (January 2022, revised October 2022) documents a 13-month learning journey (August 2020–September 2021) conducted across SDC to develop a shared institutional understanding of the triple nexus and a common way forward. The process included interviews with FDFA staff, senior management, and Swiss NGOs, plus sector dive-in workshops across peace, governance, education, and humanitarian clusters.

Key findings: SDC is already implementing nexus programmes widely but needs to mainstream nexus thinking institutionally; the peace element requires special attention; 'nexus literacy' (cross-pillar knowledge) and adaptive management are critical success factors; and no 'one-size-fits-all' nexus exists. The report proposes concrete action lines around people, processes, and partnerships, several of which were integrated into SDC's 2022 fit-for-purpose restructuring.

Title: A Mapping and Analysis of Tools and Guidance on the H-P Linkages in the HDP Nexus
Abstract:
This paper was developed by IASC Result Group 4 with pro-bono support from Interpeace. It is an inventory of guidance and tools currently available to humanitarian actors, on peace building and conflict sensitive approach, as well as an analysis on the degree to which these meet the needs of practitioners in the field. The analysis highlighted some substantial gaps in guidance and tools available to staff, but there is also a wealth of methods and in order to better understand the linkages between the peace and the humanitarian pillars of the HDPN. The paper consists of two parts.

The first part presents the analysis by Interpeace on the relevance and usefulness of currently available guidance and tools, and how these may and should be complemented in order to enhance the understanding and operationalizing of the linkages between humanitarian and peace actions. The second part consists of the mapping of available guidance and tools that relate to the peace pillar of the nexus.

Title: A Peacebuilding Tool for a Conflict-Sensitive Approach to Development: A Pilot Initiative in Nepal
Abstract:
This publication introduces the Peacebuilding Tool (PBT) — an analytical tool developed jointly by ADB, DFID, and the World Bank — and documents lessons from its pilot application in Nepal during 2010–2011. 

The PBT is designed to help project team leaders and social experts understand the local conflict context, identify risks to project implementation arising from social conflict, and formulate mitigation measures. It comprises structured questions covering the post-conflict environment, formal and informal decision-making structures, peacebuilding opportunities, and socioeconomic and geographic risk factors.

ADB and partners applied the PBT across 13 projects in 15 districts in Nepal. Key lessons include the need for ongoing analysis and flexibility as context changes, the importance of integrating findings into government systems, and the value of PBT training events for improving coordination among development partners. The publication is intended as a replicable model for other fragile and conflict-affected situations.

Title: A review of Canadian CSO experiences in Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus programming in fragile and conflict-affected countries
Abstract:
This report examines the experiences of Canadian CSOs in implementing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDP) in fragile and conflict-affected countries. The study identifies opportunities and challenges in the triple nexus approach, aiming to inform Canadian policy discussions. Analysis included literature reviews, surveys, and interviews with CSO representatives and officials from Global Affairs Canada.

Key findings highlight the increased use of the triple nexus, with special attention to gender, localization, and conflict sensitivity. Challenges include financial constraints and the need for better coordination among CSOs, local actors, and policymakers.

The report also discusses Canadian humanitarian trends, with a rise in assistance volume but a decline in its share of Real ODA. While multilateral organizations dominate assistance distribution, Canadian CSOs play a crucial role. Recommendations include strengthening CSO capacities, advocating for the triple nexus approach within GAC, and enhancing evidence bases. Engagement with policy frameworks and improving local partnerships are emphasized as crucial steps forward.

Title: A review of the triple nexus approach in discourse and practice with a focus on Islamic Relief's triple nexus programme
Abstract:
The report examines the triple nexus approach combining humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding efforts, using Islamic Relief's programme in fragile contexts as a focal point. It assesses current discourse, implementation practices, and learns from various organizations piloting triple nexus projects. Key challenges include defining the peace component, flexible financial systems, and engagement with national governments. It emphasizes that sustainable peace requires cooperation across aid sectors and warns against the politicization of humanitarian aid. 

Recommendations for Islamic Relief include clearer strategies aligning the nexus components with broader goals, embracing conflict sensitivity, investing in staff learning, and long-term collaboration with local entities. While acknowledging structural barriers, the report advocates for fundamental reforms to achieve lasting change and community resilience.

Title: Access to Durable Solutions Among IDPs in Iraq: Six Years in Displacement
Abstract: Report examining access to durable solutions — voluntary return, local integration, and settlement elsewhere — among internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Iraq following the ISIL conflict. Based on large-scale survey data, it analyses barriers and enablers to durable solutions across multiple displacement contexts in Iraq, covering shelter, livelihoods, documentation, security, social cohesion and access to services. Title: Across the Nexus: A Balancing Act for National NGOs in South Sudan
Abstract:
This Global Policy article (January 2025), part of the 'Triple Nexus: In Context and Everyday Perspective' e-book series, presents findings from PhD research with 86 interviews of South Sudanese national NGO (NNGO) representatives on how they engage with the internationally-driven HDP nexus.

Three key findings: (1) the government's role as 'project partner' creates multi-ministry complexity; (2) international actors wield disproportionate power over which organisations receive funding; and (3) communities' needs rarely align with the H/D/P silos imposed by donors. The research was conducted over 2021-2022 and contributes unique local and national actor perspectives on the nexus — a voice systematically underrepresented in the literature.

Title: Action Agenda on Internal Displacement of the UNSG Follow-Up to the Report of the UNSGs High-Level Panel on Internal Displacement
Abstract:
The United Nations Secretary-General's Action Agenda on Internal Displacement addresses the growing crisis of internal displacement driven by conflict, climate change, and disasters.

The document outlines three core goals: finding durable solutions for IDPs, preventing future displacement crises, and providing effective protection and assistance. Sustainable solutions involve reintegration, local integration, and settlement in other regions, requiring national and local leadership and UN support. A comprehensive approach involving humanitarian, development, peacebuilding, human rights, and climate change efforts is emphasized.

The agenda calls for enhanced financing strategies, private sector engagement, and improved data for solutions. Prevention efforts focus on addressing the root causes of conflict, human rights violations, and climate-related risks. The agenda stresses the need for collaboration between all stakeholders, including governments, civil society, and international actors, to ensure effective protection of IDPs and host communities and to achieve lasting impacts.

Title: Adapting in Adversity: Climate Action in Fragile and Conflict-Affected Situations
Abstract:
This Mercy Corps practitioner report (2023) examines the barriers and opportunities for climate adaptation programming in fragile and conflict-affected situations (FCS), drawing on surveys and interviews with Mercy Corps programme staff across Sub-Saharan Africa. It identifies the most significant constraints — including limited access to shock-responsive funding, governance challenges, and inflexible donor systems — while documenting innovative approaches country teams are using to overcome them. Country cases from Uganda, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Kyrgyzstan, and DRC illustrate how frontline practitioners are adapting climate programming to FCS realities.

The report argues that climate adaptation in fragile contexts is not only possible but urgently necessary, and that community-based natural resource management institutions and conflict-sensitive approaches are foundational to sustainable outcomes. Designed as a practitioner resource for those implementing at the climate-conflict-nexus interface.

Title: Addressing Everyday Complexities of the Triple Nexus: Lessons from South Sudan and Ethiopia
Abstract:
Chapter 2 of the Global Policy e-book on the triple nexus, this contribution by Wilson and Cochrane examines three key risks that emerge when the triple nexus moves from concept to practice in South Sudan and Ethiopia: (1) the nexus may strengthen donor control over local priorities; (2) it can lead to harm through poor coordination and risk transfer between organisations operating under different frameworks; and (3) it can increase operational inefficiency rather than reduce it.

Drawing on extensive field research, the authors call for strong 'guardrails' — including conflict-sensitive approaches, genuine local inclusion in decision-making, and clearer accountability mechanisms — to allow the triple nexus to live up to its promise. Essential reading for practitioners designing nexus programmes in fragile contexts.

Title: Addressing The Humanitarian-Development Nexus In The Horn of Africa
Abstract:
The report discusses the New Way of Working (NWoW) initiative aimed at bridging humanitarian and development efforts in protracted crises within the Horn of Africa, specifically targeting Somalia and Ethiopia. The NWoW seeks to enhance collaboration and coherence among these sectors, focusing on aligning short and long-term educational interventions to support recovery and development.

Despite mixed perceptions, there is a consensus on the need for improved financing models, leadership, and risk management. Education is stressed as a crucial sector requiring prioritization and resources to achieve sustainable development goals.

The report underscores the significance of multi-year planning and financing, joint analysis, and employing a multi-sectoral approach to cater to the diverse needs of affected children. It provides recommendations for better ownership of NWoW reforms, prioritization of education, and enhancing holistic programming for quality learning outcomes.

Title: Advancing Nexus in the MENA Region - Breaking the Silos
Abstract:
The report explores the operationalization of the Humanitarian, Development, and Peace (HDP) nexus approach in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, focusing on countries like Iraq, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Libya. It highlights the varying progress in integrating HDP nexus across these countries, noting challenges such as lack of clarity, inadequate coordination, and insufficient quality funding. While some strides have been made, particularly in Jordan and Palestine, structural challenges impede widespread implementation.

The report concludes with recommendations for enhancing leadership, inclusive planning, flexible multi-year funding, and better partnerships among local NGOs and other stakeholders to effectively operationalize the HDP nexus approach. Despite the set standards from the OECD\'s DAC recommendations, adherence and implementation vary significantly across countries, with more joint analysis, collaboration, and policy integration needed to achieve better humanitarian, development, and peace outcomes.

Title: Advancing the Humanitarian Development Peace Nexus Approach through Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) Global Clusters
Abstract:
The document outlines a practical approach to advancing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDPN) through the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) global clusters at the country level. It emphasizes the coordination among humanitarian, development, and peace actors to achieve collective outcomes that mitigate risks and address root causes of conflict. The nexus approach involves joint or collaborative analysis, planning, and programming while maintaining the separation of roles among actors. 

The document proposes multiple strategies and frameworks, including area-based approaches, durable solutions for internally displaced persons, and conflict sensitivity, to operationalize the nexus. It also highlights the role of governance structures and funding mechanisms to support the HDPN approach. Specific guidelines for country-level implementation are provided, alongside steps for collaborative data collection, planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes to ensure effective responses based on shared priorities.

Title: Advancing the Nexus in the MENA Region: Breaking the Silos — HDP Nexus in Iraq, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Libya
Abstract:
This 2022 research report, published by an INGO coalition, documents the state of HDP nexus operationalisation across eight selected MENA countries: Iraq, Syria (including cross-border from Turkey), Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Libya. Using desk research, perception surveys, and key informant interviews, the study identifies regional trends, critical strengths, opportunities, and structural challenges.

It finds that while Jordan and, to a lesser extent, Palestine have demonstrated meaningful progress, most MENA countries are in early nexus stages and face structural challenges around definition ambiguity, lack of institutionalisation, weak government engagement, and insufficient flexible funding. The report includes country-by-country workplan recommendations and makes a valuable contribution to the growing evidence base on nexus implementation in the Arab world.

Title: Adverse Economic Impact by Rohingya Refugees on Bangladesh: Some Way Forwards
Abstract:
This journal article examines the negative economic impact of the Rohingya refugee crisis on Bangladesh. The influx of nearly one million Rohingya refugees since 2017 poses economic, social, and environmental challenges, significantly affecting the national economy.

The government faces increased costs for health and security sectors, rising living expenses in refugee-receiving areas, local employment crises, and a drop in daily wages. Additionally, the tourism sector, particularly in Cox's Bazar, suffers from these pressures, risking long-term adverse effects on national growth. Recommendations include urgent government actions for repatriation assistance from the international community, comprehensive resource mobilization strategies, and enhanced humanitarian support for refugees to alleviate economic burdens.

The paper stresses the importance of timely, coordinated efforts to prevent further damage to Bangladesh\'s economic development objectives caused by the refugee settlement.

Title: After Assad: Navigating Syria's Humanitarian Crossroads
Abstract:
This Humanitarian Advisory Group (HAG) rapid research report (April 2025), commissioned by the UK Humanitarian Innovation Hub (UKHIH) and funded by FCDO, examines the humanitarian landscape in Syria following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.

Based on qualitative data collection in January–February 2025 including key informant interviews with local, national and international actors, it analyses the major shifts in humanitarian context, the challenge of transitioning from the cross-border 'Whole of Syria' approach to a 'One Syria' unified Damascus-based coordination structure, the risks of security vacuums and ethno-sectarian violence, and the implications for the humanitarian-development-peace nexus during Syria's critical transition period.

Title: Aid allocation across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace nexus: the role of fragility as a donors' motive
Abstract:
The article explores the role of fragility in guiding aid allocation across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus. Using the Official Development Assistance (ODA) framework, the study evaluates how donor motivations differ between self-interest, recipients' needs, merit, and fragility. Empirical analyses reveal donor heterogeneity in aid distribution, with significant variations in response to fragility depending on the aid type-humanitarian, development, or peace aid. 

Generally, humanitarian aid correlates positively with both the state and degree of fragility, while development aid shows inconsistency. Peace aid allocation more often correlates with the extent of fragility. Findings emphasize the necessity for coordinated and coherent international efforts to address fragility effectively, transcending donors' self-interest and focusing on collective impact across the HDP spectrum. The study suggests that only through cooperative frameworks can aid allocations achieve maximum effectiveness in fragile contexts.

Title: Analysing Gaps in the Humanitarian and Disaster Risk Financing Landscape
Abstract:
This policy paper analyzes the gaps in humanitarian and disaster risk financing landscapes, focusing on predictability, severity, and timing of financial flows. The paper highlights that while many crises are somewhat predictable, less than 1% of UN appeals funding utilizes pre-agreed triggers or plans. Smaller crises comprise most natural hazard-related disasters but are responsible for only a small percentage of affected individuals and funding allocation. Most humanitarian funds are spent on response rather than on anticipatory or preparedness actions, which is a critical gap.

The analysis utilizes data from multiple sources, indicating funding biases and the complexity in categorizing crises into predictable and unpredictable types. It suggests potential improvements in financing mechanisms, such as pre-agreed plans, risk pooling, and multi-year funding commitments, to better align financing with predictable and under-the-radar crises. This analysis underlines the need for better coordination and innovative financial tools to address gaps and enhance crisis responses.

Title: Annual Reports: DFI Working Group on Blended Concessional Finance for Private Sector Projects
Abstract:
The report by the DFI Working Group outlines the development and implementation of blended concessional finance to unlock private sector investment for sustainable development. The focus is on crafting common standards and transparent data practices for private sector operations, addressing market failures, and avoiding market distortion while promoting minimum concessionality and enhancing trust among stakeholders. Key outcomes include the establishment of Enhanced Principles for concessional finance, with considerations for responding to crises like COVID-19 and geopolitical conflicts.

The report highlights the significant increase in concessional commitments in sectors such as finance and infrastructure, with a focus on lower middle-income countries in regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, reflecting significant project volume increases. Challenges such as addressing climate finance, fragility in middle-income countries, and impacts stemming from the war in Ukraine are discussed alongside innovations and governance improvements to enhance concessional finance deployment. The ongoing commitment of DFIs to harmonize their efforts for greater market impact remains central through collective data analysis and sharing best practices.

Title: Applying the "Triple Nexus"; between Humanitarian, Development, and Peace in the Context of Migration Flows from Venezuela
Abstract:
This report examines the application of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus approach in responding to the Venezuelan migration crisis. The crisis exhibits a protracted nature, suggesting a need for long-term strategies, although existing interventions largely rely on short-term mechanisms due to funding constraints. Coordination through international and local platforms has improved, but common strategic objectives remain insufficiently defined. Local organizations initially played significant roles but are now overshadowed by international actors, limiting internal ownership of disaster responses. Increasing engagement with diaspora organizations is noted, yet concerns about political biases persist. While the triple nexus approach is recognized as suitable, substantial gaps remain in its operational implementation.

Humanitarian aid, addressing basic needs of migrants, still dominates in priority. Development initiatives focus on socio-economic integration, legal support, and regularization, yet face challenges due to resource constraints and regulatory obstacles. The peacebuilding component seeks to address xenophobia and promote cultural integration, but its practical impact is questioned. Recommendations emphasize the need for multi-year funding, enhanced coordination, and a stronger focus on conflict sensitivity, sustainability, and community involvement.

Abstract:

Using a Developmental Evaluation approach, the study draws on in-country data collection in Mexico, Mauritania, and Mozambique, desk-based research for Niger, Ethiopia, and Uganda, and workshops with UNHCR and GIZ staff.

Key findings cover partnership enablers and constraints, operationalisation of peace outcomes (often underinvested), and lessons on complementarity with World Bank investments. The study offers recommendations tailored to BMZ, GIZ, UNHCR, and other stakeholders.

Title: Applying the HDP Nexus in Education: promoting sustained and equitable access in fragile crisis contexts
Abstract:
The policy paper discusses the application of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus in education, focusing on fragile contexts like Burkina Faso and Mozambique. The document emphasizes the integration of humanitarian aid, development planning, and peacebuilding in education programs as vital for addressing vulnerability drivers, promoting social cohesion, and building peaceful societies. Key challenges include lack of operational understanding of the HDP Nexus, structural inequalities, limited local ownership, and disconnect between local realities and global frameworks.

Recommendations for donors and policymakers advocate for long-term, flexible financing, peace-oriented education programs, local leadership, and improved coordination between local and global actors. Case studies from Burkina Faso and Mozambique highlight successful initiatives in conflict-sensitive education and community-led disaster risk reduction. The paper underscores the need for inclusive, context-sensitive education systems that empower communities and support sustainable peace.

Title: Beyond Relief: Securing Livelihoods and Agency for Rohingya Refugees in Bangladesh
Abstract:
This policy paper explores the challenges faced by Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, particularly those in Cox's Bazar, in securing livelihoods and maintaining agency amidst economic hardship and limited resources.

The research underscores how refugees, while receiving aid, often rely on non-aid resources like remittances and temporary work to meet their needs, reflecting their active efforts to support their families. It highlights the prevalence of family separation and debilitating debt among camp residents. Despite receiving basic food assistance, refugees struggle with expenses for health, education, and communication, accentuated by restrictions on movement, employment, and internet usage.

The paper argues for policy shifts to increase refugees' economic self-reliance, improve communication networks, and engage refugees in planning humanitarian aid. It stresses the importance of creating real livelihood opportunities which could benefit both refugees and host communities by reducing tensions and illegal migration triggers. The paper calls for greater international involvement and consideration of regional dynamics to address the complex situation affecting displaced Rohingya families.

Title: Beyond the Box: Rethinking the Nexus for a Changing World
Abstract: Chapter 7 of the Global Policy triple nexus e-book, this contribution shifts from macro discourse to examine what the HDP nexus demands from the internal organisational structures of international NGOs. The author argues that the nexus, as a donor-driven policy instrument, is designed to address problems created by the very system it seeks to reform — and that meaningful nexus implementation requires going deeper: confronting one's own organisation, leadership, colleagues, and administrative structures that stifle progress. The piece examines how grassroots organisations embedded in the international aid framework often find nexus policy debates disconnected from their daily working realities, and argues that the nexus must be reclaimed from its macro policy framing and reconstructed around local realities and organisational transformation. A provocative and practically grounded perspective for INGO practitioners.

Title: Beyond the Crisis: Strengthening Nexus Coherence for Social Protection in the Occupied Palestinian Territory
Abstract: This ILO article (July 2024) documents how humanitarian and development actors working on social assistance in the Occupied Palestinian Territory maintained and accelerated nexus coordination despite the October 2023 outbreak of war in Gaza. Drawing on lessons from the Social Protection, Cash and Voucher Assistance Thematic Working Group (SPCVA TWG) — co-chaired by the Ministry of Social Development and OCHA — it shows how trust built over two years of nexus-oriented coordination prevented the approach from collapsing under extreme stress. Key lessons: flexible donor funding is essential; coordination must be institutionalised before crises hit; and the SPCVA TWG model enabled humanitarian actors to engage in development forums and vice versa. Notably relevant as a nexus resilience story in the most constrained of operating environments.

Title: BRAC in Bangladesh and beyond: bridging the humanitarian-development nexus through localisation
Abstract:
This journal article explores the evolution and impact of BRAC, a non-governmental organization from Bangladesh, which has successfully bridged the humanitarian-development nexus through local community empowerment. BRAC's approach, deeply rooted in Bangladesh\'s socio-political history and its philosophy of vernacular humanitarianism, focuses on integrating emergency relief with long-term developmental objectives. 

The article examines BRAC's global expansion and adaptation of its model in countries like Afghanistan and Sri Lanka, highlighting challenges in managing expectations and maintaining cultural sensitivity. BRAC's reputation for combining humanitarian aid and development has positioned it as a leading actor in humanitarian responses like the Rohingya refugee crisis.

The article also scrutinizes the concept of localization in humanitarian aid, bringing to light the tension between BRAC's identity as a local and international actor and its role in advocating for local empowerment and decision-making. Ultimately, BRAC's strategies emphasize learning from local contexts and integrating humanitarian and developmental goals, offering significant insights for both localization and the nexus between humanitarian and development sectors.

Title: Breaking boundaries: local and national actors' engagement in the humanitarian-development-peace nexus
Abstract:
The report, authored by Dorothy Mae Albiento, explores local and national actors' (LNAs) engagement in the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus. It highlights the integration of these three sectors in LNA programming, emphasizing community engagement, gender inclusion, and peace-building, in contrast to the segmented approach of international actors.

The study draws insights from surveys and interviews with LNAs across 22 countries, identifying how LNAs' proximity to communities allows them to address short-term and long-term needs flexibly. Challenges include siloed funding and complex donor requirements, which restrict effective implementation. The report calls for enhanced international support for LNAs, advocating for flexible financing, inclusion in decision-making, and better measurement of program impacts.

Recommendations focus on showcasing LNA practices, involving them in global strategy design, and increasing direct funding to LNAs to support sustainable, holistic solutions.

Abstract:

Title: Bridging the Divide [Arabic]: A Guide to Implementing the HDP Nexus for Health (Second Edition)
Abstract:
Despite growing consensus on the value of the humanitarian development and peace nexus (HDPNx) approach also known as the New Way of Working practical guidance on how to apply it effectively in the health sector has long been lacking. The HDPNx approach seeks to leverage the comparative advantages of different actors to improve efficiency and sustainability reduce duplication and service delivery gaps address the root causes of emergencies and support transitions from humanitarian response to stabilization recovery and development. To address this gap this guide was developed as a practical tool to support the implementation of the HDPNx approach in health-related contexts.

The first edition published in 2020 aimed to help health actors operationalize the approach in a coordinated multisectoral manner. Since then advances in both understanding and application of the approach have emerged. This second edition builds on the foundation of the original guide incorporating recent developments and operational learning to ensure continued relevance and effectiveness.

Title: Bridging the Fragility Gap: Climate Action in Fragile and Conflict-Affected Situations
Abstract: This Mercy Corps report (May 2025) addresses two interrelated challenges: how to increase climate adaptation investments in fragile and conflict-affected situations (FCS), and how to spend such funding on interventions that actually work. Drawing on perspectives from bilateral donors, international financial institutions, peer organisations, and Mercy Corps programme teams in Colombia, Iraq, Kenya, Somalia, and Uganda, the report identifies concrete recommendations to better align climate finance and programming for underserved communities on the frontlines of the climate crisis. It argues that while the fragility barriers to climate finance are real, they are not insurmountable — and examines how conflict-sensitive, flexible, and locally-anchored programme approaches can deliver adaptation outcomes even in the most challenging contexts. Abstract:
This paper examines how organisations can build the institutional capacity required to implement conflict-sensitive practice systematically and effectively. It goes beyond individual staff training to address the organisational systems, structures, policies and cultures needed to embed conflict sensitivity throughout an institution. Key dimensions addressed include: leadership and management commitment to conflict sensitivity; human resources and staff capacities; programme systems and tools for conflict sensitivity; monitoring and accountability frameworks; and organisational learning.

Title: Building peace, building states? Examining the Humanitarian – Development – Peace Nexus in Colombia's PDET regions
Abstract:
This academic publication, listed through Duke University Scholars, examines the intersection between the humanitarian-development-peace nexus and state-building processes in fragile and conflict-affected settings. The nexus framework is inherently political: its emphasis on supporting national authorities, building national capacities, and aligning international assistance with national plans inevitably involves engagement with processes of state formation and state legitimacy.

The paper interrogates what it means to 'build states' through nexus approaches — examining whether the nexus reinforces, challenges, or reconfigures existing state-society relationships in fragile contexts. It analyses the tensions between humanitarian principles of independence and neutrality and the nexus's implicit state-centric orientation, and asks whether the nexus framework adequately accounts for the contested, partial, and sometimes predatory nature of the states with which it engages.

Drawing on theoretical frameworks from international relations and peace studies alongside empirical evidence from nexus implementation, the paper contributes to scholarly debates about the political economy of the triple nexus.

Title: Can Market Approaches Catalyze Self-Reliance for Forcibly Displaced and Host Populations?
Abstract:
This journal article examines the potential of market systems approaches to foster self-reliance among forcibly displaced and host populations. As the number of refugees globally reaches staggering proportions and displacement becomes increasingly protracted, traditional aid dependency is unsustainable. Various constraints faced by forcibly displaced populations, such as lack of legal status, limited access to finance, and sociocultural challenges, hinder successful market integration. 

The article emphasizes the need for systems-based solutions that address both displaced and host communities' challenges, while promoting economic opportunities and inclusive growth. Recommendations include conducting detailed assessments to understand target populations, using trusted intermediaries, creatively partnering with refugee-led organizations, and combining direct interventions with broader systemic approaches.

Through case studies and program examples, it illustrates successful strategies to empower displaced populations economically, suggesting ways to overcome barriers and optimize participation in host markets.

Title: Capacity and complementarity in the Rohingya response in Bangladesh
Abstract:
This paper examines capacity and complementarity in the humanitarian response to the Rohingya refugee crisis in Cox\'s Bazar, Bangladesh, following the mass displacement from Myanmar in 2017. It outlines the roles of various stakeholders, including refugees, host communities, state actors, local/national humanitarian actors, and international organizations. Local and national actors have significant capacity in disaster response, but responding to the refugee crisis requires specific humanitarian and protection capacities. Capacity is perceived differently by stakeholders, with international actors viewed as having technical and financial resources, and local actors offering contextual knowledge.

Capacity strengthening through training is common, although it overlooks structural challenges and power dynamics that hinder capacity actualization. Complementarity is limited by parallel coordination systems, divergent objectives, funding constraints, and power imbalances between local and international actors. While isolated instances of complementarity exist, broader efforts are needed to foster cooperation and leverage the strengths of all actors to support effective humanitarian outcomes for affected communities.

Title: Case study: Operationalising the 'triple nexus'
Abstract:
The report, produced by Altai Consulting for the European Union, provides an overview of the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus, or 'triple nexus,' relevant to the European Union Emergency Trust Fund for Africa (EUTF). Through interviews with various stakeholders, the study addresses the HDP nexus\'s effectiveness in coordinating humanitarian, development, and peace actions.

Highlighting initiatives in regions like the Sahel, Lake Chad, Horn of Africa, and North Africa, the report notes the emerging frameworks and programs aimed at aligning actions across sectors. Despite advances, integrating the peace component remains challenging due to risks perceived around operational neutrality.

The report suggests improving coordination through joint analysis and planning, addressing funding cycles misalignments, and stressing the importance of empowering local actors and considering gender and climate change in nexus strategies. Lessons learned are aimed at enhancing coordination and strategic outcomes across the HDP spheres.

Abstract:
This CEIPAZ analytical note (February 2025) examines the UN Security Council's annual open debate on Women, Peace and Security (WPS), held under the theme 'Women Build Peace in a Changing Environment'. Drawing on the statements of the UN Deputy Secretary-General and UN Women Executive Director, the note documents the alarming global regression on WPS implementation documented in the Secretary-General's 2024 report on Resolution 1325.

It highlights the growing backlash against gender terminology and equality commitments by some governments, and its consequences for UN and civil society work. The note is part of the CEIPAZ project on WPS and the HDP triple nexus in Spanish cooperation.

Abstract:
This CEIPAZ analytical note (April 2025) examines the triple nexus (HDP) approach from a gender perspective, arguing that integrating gender equality into humanitarian action, development, and peacebuilding is essential to ensure sustainable peace and effective interventions.

The note situates the gender perspective within the OECD DAC Recommendation and traces the historical evolution of the nexus from the double to the triple nexus. It addresses current challenges including funding fragmentation, tensions between humanitarian principles and political objectives, and the critical role of gender-sensitive conflict analysis.

Written in Spanish as part of the CEIPAZ WPS-HDP project, this is the Spanish-language companion to the CEIPAZ English Review Paper on the same theme.

Abstract: This CEIPAZ analytical note (2025) examines the convergence of the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda and humanitarian action, tracing the evolution of gender integration in humanitarian response from ECOSOC resolutions to the Call to Action on Gender-Based Violence in Emergencies. The note documents how gender-based violence — particularly sexual violence in conflict — has been increasingly integrated into the WPS framework through successive Security Council resolutions (1820, 1888, 1960, 2016), and analyses remaining gaps in funding and implementation. It argues for stronger convergence between the WPS and humanitarian agendas within the triple nexus framework. Part of the CEIPAZ WPS-HDP project in Spanish cooperation.

Abstract:
This CEIPAZ analytical note (2025), prepared by researchers from Gernika Gogoratuz, the University of Coimbra, and CEAP (Cabo Delgado), offers a critical analysis of triple nexus implementation in northern Mozambique from a feminist and decolonial perspective. It is based on experience presented at the CEIPAZ seminar on WPS and the HDP nexus in Spanish cooperation.

The note argues that the dominant triple nexus approaches remain top-down, reproduce unequal power relations and Western intervention models, and fail to incorporate local knowledge and community agency — particularly that of grassroots women. It calls for a fundamental rethinking of the nexus from the perspective of community agendas and local capacity strengthening, moving beyond colonial and paternalistic frameworks. A rare critical, feminist, and decolonial voice in the Spanish-language nexus literature.

Abstract: This CEIPAZ Review Paper (October 2025) provides a comprehensive analysis of the triple nexus (HDP) approach through a gender lens, examining how integrating the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda into nexus programming can improve equity and effectiveness. The paper traces the historical evolution from the 'double nexus' to the triple nexus, and argues that a gender perspective is an essential cross-cutting issue for ensuring that women, girls and other vulnerable groups are addressed as agents of change — not merely beneficiaries — in humanitarian action, development, and peacebuilding. It situates its analysis within the OECD DAC Recommendation and the UNSC Resolution 1325 framework, and explores current challenges including tensions between humanitarian principles and political objectives, and the fragmentation of gender-responsive financing. Title: Changing People's Lives from Delivering Aid to Ending Need
Abstract:

It commits humanitarian and development actors to implement a 'New Way of Working' that meets immediate humanitarian needs while simultaneously reducing risk and vulnerability and working towards collective outcomes that support the achievement of the 2030 Agenda. 

The document articulates the paradigm shift required: moving from siloed, short-term humanitarian and development programming to integrated, multi-year approaches with a greater diversity of partners. It calls for putting affected people at the centre, anticipating rather than just reacting to crises, and developing national systems rather than parallel delivery structures.

Title: Climate Action in Conflict and Fragile Settings: Closing the Implementation Gap
Abstract:
This ICRC blog post (November 2024) reflects on progress — and the continuing gap — in climate action for conflict and fragile settings, written at the onset of COP29. The authors review the COP28 Declaration on Climate, Relief, Recovery and Peace — signed by over 80 states and 40 organisations — and assess how far political commitments have been translated into tangible outcomes. They argue that climate change and conflict compound each other: conflict worsens communities' adaptive capacity while climate stress intensifies conflict risks.

The piece examines structural barriers — institutional aversion to risk, inability to programme in insecure areas, and mismatch between climate fund design and fragile governance contexts — and proposes practical pathways including fit-for-purpose financing instruments and stronger HDP-climate nexus coordination. Directly relevant for practitioners and policymakers working at the intersection of climate, peace, and humanitarian action.

Abstract:
This 115-page CGIAR research report (2024), conducted under the CGIAR Initiative on Fragility, Conflict, and Migration (FCM), explores the intersections of climate resilience, displacement, and development within the HDP nexus framework in Jordan — one of the world's most water-scarce countries and largest refugee-hosting nations per capita.

The study examines how rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, and increasing droughts exacerbate existing vulnerabilities in a context of rapid population growth driven by refugee influxes. It provides evidence-based recommendations for fostering climate resilience and social cohesion in fragile settings affected by protracted displacement, drawing on the Anticipatory Approaches in Host Communities for Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Mitigation (AHEAD) research in Irbid and Ramtha municipalities.

Title: Co-ordination across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:

Co-ordination is the first pillar of the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) Recommendation on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus adopted by the DAC in 2019. Effective co-ordination is critical to the success of HDP Nexus approaches.

However, despite a limited donor base and implementing entities, challenges persist in co-ordinating actions across humanitarian, development, and peace sectors. Title: Coherence in Conflict: Bringing Humanitarian and Development Aid Streams Together
Abstract:
This paper examines the practical challenge of achieving coherence between humanitarian and development aid streams in conflict-affected contexts, drawing on case study evidence. It analyses the systemic, institutional and operational barriers that prevent humanitarian and development actors from effectively coordinating and working towards shared objectives.

Key themes include: structural funding differences between humanitarian and development aid; conflicting mandates and principles; the challenge of transitioning from crisis response to long-term development; and the conditions under which coherence is achievable. The paper provides recommendations for donors, UN agencies and NGOs on how to create enabling conditions for more coherent programming in conflict settings.

Abstract:
The brief outlines the collaborative efforts between UNDP and UNHCR from 2023-2025 to address issues related to forcibly displaced and stateless persons through the integration of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The collaboration aims to enhance access to livelihoods, uphold the rule of law, and improve governance across national and local institutions within the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus. 

Key projects include initiatives in Myanmar to facilitate refugee returns with recovery and resilience-focused activities and the Regional Refugee and Resilience Plan (3RP) to manage the Syrian crisis impact in countries like Turkey, Lebanon, and Jordan. Collaboration in countries such as Burkina Faso and Colombia seeks to promote durable solutions, social cohesion, and improve living conditions in host communities affected by displacement and insecurity.

The collaboration underlines the significance of international cooperation, shared responsibility, and innovative financing to address the drivers of forced displacement and support peacebuilding efforts worldwide.

Sida has enhanced resilience and nexus capacities, established a nexus committee, and developed guidance to advance HDP priorities, particularly in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Mozambique, Burkina Faso, and other nations. Emphasis is placed on aligning programming with risks, building resilience, and fostering durable solutions for displaced populations. 

Sida's strategies include coordination among agencies and donors, flexibility in programming, and prioritization of local context. Challenges include adapting to rapidly changing situations, integrating peace components into the nexus, and overcoming coordination hurdles. Embedded lessons underscore the importance of comprehensive planning, conflict sensitivity, and adaptable management frameworks for sustainable impact.

Abstract:

The manual outlines steps for assessing organizational readiness, allocating resources, and developing conflict-sensitive principles. It also provides tools for conflict analysis, such as conflict trees, conflict maps, and stakeholder profiles, enabling organizations to better address conflict causes and effects.

Title: Connecting Disasters and Climate Change to the Humanitarian- Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:
This journal article argues for integrating climate change into the existing humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus instead of establishing it as a separate stream. The authors contend that climate change impacts should be embedded within the framework of disaster risk reduction (DRR), and these components must work together as part of existing humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding efforts.

The article identifies risks in segregating climate change as a standalone aspect and highlights the importance of addressing climate impacts within the broader context of vulnerability reduction. The authors suggest that focusing on integrating climate change adaptation, mitigation, and disaster risk reduction into the HDP nexus can offer a comprehensive strategy to tackle root causes of vulnerability.

This integrated approach leverages existing frameworks like the Sendai Framework, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change agreements, and the Sustainable Development Goals to enhance the collective impact on reducing vulnerability and promoting resilience.

The paper outlines principles and operational challenges, emphasizing the importance of context-specific engagement, conflict sensitivity, and respecting the varying mandates of different actors. It discusses the peace aspect of the nexus, noting the potential issues of integrating humanitarian principles with political objectives.

The paper further explores operational steps like joint context analysis, planning, coordination, funding, and adaptive management, offering examples from countries like Nigeria, Myanmar, and Cameroon. Title: Country Brief on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Haiti
Abstract:
The Country Brief on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus in Haiti highlights the nation's political, economic, and social instability from 2017 to 2022, exacerbated by violence and natural disasters. Despite recognizing the importance of integrating humanitarian aid, development, and peacebuilding efforts, Haiti faces challenges in operationalizing this nexus due to insufficient funding and weak partner dynamics.

The nexus approach has been central to discussions for the last 3-4 years, aiming at joint analysis and coordinated actions. Efforts are being made to align the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) with Haiti's strategic plans for 2030. Key challenges include data collection limitations and erosion of social cohesion.

Good practices involve structural responses addressing immediate needs and synchronized efforts through internal sessions. Financing debates focus on attracting donors to support comprehensive strategies encompassing peacebuilding and sustainable development, despite existing hurdles. Local actors, including women and youth organizations, are integral in identifying priorities and executing programs. Collaboration among international donors and engaging local actors are emphasized to streamline HDP nexus efforts and ensure inclusive, culturally sensitive programming.

Title: COVID 19 and conflict sensitivity: Rapid Operational Conflict Risk and Prevention Tool
Abstract:
The World Food Programme (WFP) released a report on the operational challenges posed by COVID-19, focusing on conflict sensitivity. The report identifies risks emerging from national responses to the pandemic, highlighting potential for heightened tensions and social unrest due to differential responses and the politicization of aid.

The report outlines a Rapid Operational Conflict Risk Tool that includes key questions designed to help identify and mitigate these risks, supporting conflict-sensitive programming adjustments. Mitigation measures suggested include enhancing transparency in targeting vulnerable groups and fostering trust and social cohesion. The involvement of security forces and misinformation are flagged as factors exacerbating tensions.

Overall, the report underscores the risk of COVID-19 exacerbating existing conflicts and tensions, while also providing opportunities to support peace and social cohesion through tailored programming and diagnostics sessions.

Title: Critical Evolutions in the Peacebuilding-Development Praxis Nexus: Crisis and Complexity, Synergy and Transformation
Abstract:
This article reflects on paradigmatic shifts in the peacebuilding-development nexus over the two decades since Peter Uvin's landmark 2002 analysis. Drawing on desk research and the author's experience within the UN system and civil society, it maps evolving praxis paradigms across the nexus in response to growing crisis complexity, incorporating fragility, violence, and humanitarian crisis.

The article identifies paradigms with continuing relevance (development axiomatically reduces conflict, conditionality, human security), adapted paradigms (conflict prevention and sustaining peace, peacebuilding in development, global and national system transformation), and prominent new paradigms (statebuilding and social contracts, inclusion, and the triple nexus). It argues that the complexity facing the fields demands inter-paradigm learning, pluralism, and synergy, and that the HDP Nexus's potential success relies on addressing structural causes and drivers of conflict, fragility, and crisis at both national and transnational levels.

Abstract:

The briefing covers the period from November 2022 to mid-2023 and reflects on progress achieved in building a field-based coordination mechanism among UN agencies, international and national NGOs. Title: DAC Recommendation on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:
This updated OECD DAC Recommendation on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (2025) builds on the original 2019 Recommendation that established a common standard for coherent action by DAC members in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

The 2025 update reflects five years of implementation learning, monitoring, and adaptation, incorporating new evidence and adjusting the 11 guiding principles in response to emerging challenges including climate change, COVID-19 recovery, and evolving conflict dynamics.

It provides DAC members and UN adherents with updated guidance on coordination, programming, and financing across the HDP nexus, and serves as a living policy framework for collective action to address the root causes of humanitarian crises.

Title: Danish Refugee Council Case Study: A Localized Approach to Nexus Programming
Abstract:
The Danish Refugee Council Case Study focuses on a localized approach to nexus programming in the Liptako-Gourma region, significantly impacted by insecurity and humanitarian crises. The report highlights the need for multi-sectoral responses due to intertwined humanitarian, developmental, and peace challenges. It emphasizes the value local civil society organizations (CSOs) bring to partnerships through their knowledge of socio-cultural contexts and relationships with local communities.

Key challenges identified include lack of trust and inclusion between international NGOs (INGOs) and CSOs, complicated procedures, limited funding, and power imbalances. The DRC aims to establish equitable, strategic partnerships with CSOs rooted in diverse representation and long-term collaboration. Through integrated programming, the DRC seeks to address vulnerabilities by embedding cross-cutting skills like security and gender into consortia and promoting shared accountability. Successful implementation requires INGOs to invest adequately and share power with CSOs to enable real collaboration and co-ownership of projects aimed at addressing both immediate needs and fostering resilience and social cohesion.

Title: Decent Work across the HDP Nexus in the Arab Region: Workshop Report and Recommendations
Abstract:
This ILO final report documents the outcomes of a four-day workshop (9–12 September 2024, Amman, Jordan) co-organised by ILO and the UNDP Nexus Academy, with Sida support. Bringing together senior HDP practitioners and policymakers from Yemen, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, and the Occupied Palestinian Territory, the workshop developed concrete recommendations for promoting decent work within the HDP nexus at country level.

Key themes included: integrating humanitarian cash programming with social protection system-building; transitioning short-term livelihood support into peace-responsive employment; the PROSPECTS partnership model (ILO, UNICEF, UNHCR, WB, IFC) as a nexus financing example; and the critical and underrecognised role of trade unions and employers' organisations as nexus coordination actors. Country-level workplans were developed as follow-up outputs.

Title: Defining a Humanitarian Shelter and Settlements Research Agenda
Abstract:
This journal article presents a research agenda for humanitarian shelter and settlements, addressing knowledge gaps crucial for practitioners. Despite advances in post-disaster sheltering over the past decades, there's still a disconnect between evidence needed and research produced.

The authors gathered a Delphi panel of experts to define and prioritize research areas, identifying 96 needs across six themes: approaches to sheltering, programming, design and construction, impacts and outcomes, disaster risk reduction and humanitarian-development nexus, and challenging contexts. Priorities include understanding self-recovery, long-term impacts, and transition from response to recovery.

The article emphasizes the need for evidence to align humanitarian response with developmental goals and faced growing challenges like protracted crises, climate change, and urbanization, necessitating reforms in standards, funding, and practices in the sector.

Title: Deploying a Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus Approach: Exploring, Strengthening and Reviving Dryland Ecosystems
Abstract:
This FAO-CARE-CGIAR joint discussion paper (2021) examines how the HDP nexus can be operationalised in dryland contexts — regions disproportionately affected by climate shocks, environmental degradation, and conflict.

The paper evaluates 18 projects across dryland areas, highlighting the importance of conflict sensitivity, climate change monitoring and resilience, food and nutrition security, and attention to vulnerable people including pastoralists, IDPs, and women. It proposes four key nexus actions for drylands: inclusive targeting, conflict risk reduction, climate change adaptation integration, and enhanced monitoring.

The paper makes the case that addressing climate change, land degradation, and conflict together — rather than in silos — can lead to game-changing solutions for dryland communities, and contributes to the growing climate-conflict-nexus evidence base.

Title: Development actors at the nexus: Lessons from crises in Bangladesh, Cameroon and Somalia
Abstract:
This report explores the role of development actors in addressing protracted humanitarian crises in Bangladesh, Cameroon, and Somalia, emphasizing the operationalization of the 'triple nexus' of humanitarian, development, and peace actions. It identifies five key areas: partnerships, coordination and joined-up planning, programming approaches, financing tools, and organizational issues.

Key findings highlight the importance of effective partnerships with governments and local actors, challenges in coordination due to weak integration between humanitarian and development actions, and varied success in embedding risk and resilience into programming. Financing mechanisms and instruments tailored to crisis contexts are crucial for supporting the vulnerable populations, yet they remain underutilized and poorly integrated. Organizational changes are necessary to break down silos within agencies and enhance decentralized decision-making.

The report underscores the need for further research and development of coherent strategies and systems to better align the efforts across the humanitarian, development, and peace sectors.

Title: Development Co-operation Report 2024: Tackling Poverty and Inequalities through the Green Transition
Abstract:
This annual OECD Development Co-operation Report provides policymakers with evidence, data and insights on how development co-operation can tackle poverty and inequalities in the context of the global green transition.

The report argues that amid the urgency of climate action, development co-operation providers risk losing sight of a deepening poverty and inequality crisis in low- and middle-income countries. It presents new analysis showing that poverty and inequality must be addressed together, rather than in isolation, and identifies three cross-cutting policy priorities: raising ambitions on poverty and inequality reduction, increasing development and green finance, and ensuring human rights and social standards in green transitions. The report also reviews proven policies including social protection expansion, tax system reform, and labour market policies.

Title: Development Discourse and Global History: From Colonialism to the Sustainable Development Goals
Abstract:
This book uses the archaeological and genealogical methods of Michel Foucault to trace the origins of development discourse back to late colonialism, noting significant discontinuities that led to the establishment of a new development discourse and its accompanying industry.

It describes the contestations, appropriations, and transformations of the concept of development over time, showing how trends since the 1980s crisis — including emphasis on participation and ownership, sustainable development, and free markets — contain Eurocentric, authoritarian, and depoliticizing elements, while also recognizing progressive appropriations.

The author concludes by analysing old and new features of development discourse in the debate on the Sustainable Development Goals and discussing the contribution of discourse analysis to development studies. The book is aimed at researchers and students in development studies, global history, and discourse analysis.

Title: Disarming hunger: the role of peace within Humanitarian-Development-Peace nexus approaches in addressing food crises
Abstract:
The outcome document from the Stockholm Forum on Peace and Development 2023 highlights the critical role of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus in addressing food crises, particularly in conflict-affected regions where acute food insecurity is prevalent due to disruptions in access, markets, and transportation. The discussions emphasize the interconnection between hunger and conflict, advocating for a holistic approach that leverages peace for positive food security outcomes.

Key recommendations include enhancing funding mechanisms for local actors, integrating diverse stakeholders in resilience programming, and leveraging food systems for peace and social cohesion. Localizing interventions and empowering grassroots capacities are crucial for effective action, emphasizing the need for international actors to recognize local capabilities and mitigating risks. This underscores the importance of integrating and understanding local contexts and dynamics to tailor interventions appropriately.

Title: Dissolving the Difference Between Humanitarianism and Development: The Mixing of a Rights-Based Solution
Abstract:
This essay by Hugo Slim argues that the conventional distinction between humanitarianism and development is misconceived and unhelpful. Drawing on examples from Rwanda and Kenya, the author contends that both sectors share the same fundamental value — belief in human dignity and equality — and that the false dichotomy between them was an artefact of Cold War politics.

The paper traces how international humanitarian law and human rights law share common origins, and how a rights-based approach to both humanitarianism and development dissolves the artificial divide. It calls for aid workers across sectors to recognise themselves as human rights workers united by a common ethic.

Title: Doing Nexus Differently: How can Humanitarian and Development Actors link or integrate humanitarian action, development, and peace?
Abstract:
The report, 'Doing Nexus Differently,' focuses on the integration of humanitarian action, development, and peace through the Nexus approach in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. It emphasizes the need for localized, bottom-up strategies to enhance resilience, address root causes of conflict, and promote women\'s empowerment. Key challenges include the difficulty of aligning funding streams and organizational structures to support integrated, flexible programming.

The report advocates for a Double/Triple Nexus approach, showcasing successful cases where merging these sectors led to community empowerment and sustainable development. It highlights the importance of adaptive management, local participation, and evidence-based analysis to avoid potential pitfalls like politicization of aid. Critically, it stresses gender equality and the inclusion of women\'s voices in Nexus programming. CARE calls for regional and global partnerships to influence Nexus practices and ensure long-term, empowered community involvement.

Identifies the structural barriers — earmarked funding, incompatible planning cycles, and separate institutional mandates — that have historically prevented coherent engagement, tracing the origins of challenges that subsequent reform efforts including the Grand Bargain and the OECD DAC Recommendation on the HDP Nexus have sought to address.

Title: Dorcas Strategic plan 2026-2030: Local power creates lasting change
Abstract:
This is the 2026–2030 strategic plan of Dorcas, a Dutch Christian international development and humanitarian organisation operating in more than 20 fragile and crisis-affected countries. The strategic plan articulates Dorcas's vision for the next five years under the overarching theme 'Local power creates lasting change' — reflecting a fundamental organisational commitment to shifting power and resources to local and national actors as the primary agents of humanitarian, development and peacebuilding work. 

The plan outlines Dorcas's strategic priorities across its three core programme areas — emergency response, resilience building, and long-term development — as well as its approach to the humanitarian-development-peace nexus as an integrated way of working. It describes how Dorcas intends to strengthen local partnerships, invest in local capacity, advocate for more equitable funding flows to local actors, and embed conflict sensitivity and gender equality across all its programming. 

The plan reflects broader trends in the sector towards locally-led humanitarian and development action, and positions Dorcas as a partnership organisation that accompanies local change rather than directing it.

Title: Durable Solutions and the Humanitarian-Development Nexus: A Literature Review
Abstract:
This literature review by Merve Erdilmen, published by the Local Engagement Refugee Research Network (LERRN), examines the scholarly and policy literature at the intersection of durable solutions for refugees and the humanitarian-development nexus. It covers the traditional trio of durable solutions (repatriation, local integration, resettlement), emerging alternative pathways (mobility, self-reliance, transnational networks), intersectional and gender-sensitive approaches, and the policies of major international organizations including UNHCR, IOM, UNDP and the World Bank.

The paper identifies three key gaps: the link between durable solutions and the humanitarian-development nexus is underexplored; literature has an 'exilic bias' focusing on displacement rather than solutions; and most research focuses on the Global North rather than the Global South where most refugees reside.

The program operationalises a development approach to the refugee crisis, demonstrating how development financing mechanisms can complement humanitarian assistance to support self-reliance, formal employment, and economic integration of displaced populations.

Title: Ecosystem Assessment of Food, Land, and Water Actors in the Humanitarian, Development, and Peace Nexus
Abstract:
The CGIAR Initiative on Fragility, Conflict, and Migration conducts an ecosystem assessment on Food, Land, and Water Systems (FLWS) within the Humanitarian, Development, and Peace (HDP) Nexus across 14 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. The evaluation highlights the challenges faced by the 1.5 billion people living in Fragility and Conflict-Affected Settings (FCAS) due to food insecurity and poverty traps.

The report identifies over 600 innovators, focusing predominantly on food production with an emphasis on strengthening innovation through private sector funding, public-private partnerships, and international involvement. However, the ecosystem remains nascent, with innovations predominantly concentrated in food production and underrepresentation in areas like water resources and migrant services.

Recommendations include prioritizing local actors, better coordination with research organizations, context-specific innovations, and substantial private sector engagement to achieve sustainable growth in the FCAS markets.

Abstract:
This IECAH study (2025), supported by AECID's Office of Humanitarian Action, analyses the implementation of the triple nexus (TN) approach in Colombia — a country grappling with decades of armed conflict, forced displacement, and the current 'paz total' (total peace) process. Using mixed methods including field research and interviews with actors from local to international level, the study documents advances, obstacles, and proposals for strengthening the nexus.

Key findings highlight the need for flexible financing, better cross-sectoral coordination, more effective gender mainstreaming, and stronger community leadership. Title: Employment and Decent Work in the Humanitarian Development Peace Nexus
Abstract:
