Abstract:
This Global Policy journal contribution from UNDP examines the critical role of women as peacebuilders within HDP nexus programming, drawing on practical case studies from the Philippines and Somalia. It argues that women's meaningful participation in peace processes increases the likelihood of lasting peace agreements by up to 35%, with ripple effects across community resilience and nexus linkages. 

In the Bangsamoro region of the Philippines, the Women's Institute for Peace – Rido Ayad Multi-Purpose Association (WIM-RAMP) demonstrates how women's leadership in conflict prevention can anchor nexus efforts locally.

In Somalia, UNDP-supported Alternative Dispute Resolution centres show how empowering women through access to justice contributes to social cohesion.

Title: Enhancing gender equality and women's empowerment in the Humanitarian-Development-Peace nexus in countries affected by the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Abstract:
The brief examines the implementation of the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda in countries affected by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, focusing on Georgia, Poland, Republic of Moldova, Romania, Slovakia, and Ukraine. It explores the integration of the WPS agenda within the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus, emphasizing the advancement of gender equality and women's empowerment amid collaborative partnerships. 

Key aspects include gender-sensitive analyses and comprehensive approaches to humanitarian response, development, and peacebuilding. The brief highlights the importance of National Action Plans (NAPs) for implementing WPS agenda pillars and integrating gender perspectives into the HDP nexus, alongside the challenges faced such as limited representation, fragmented coordination, and insufficient data. It discusses the role of feminist foreign policy and suggests ways forward for effective gender-responsive integration of refugees and coordination among regional actors.

Recommendations include boosting women's participation, coordinating resources and efforts, and advancing multi-stakeholder regional dialogues for more inclusive, resilient societies. Efforts to improve policy coherence, joint planning, and financing are deemed essential for addressing conflict and building peace.

Title: Enough Theory! A Somali Consortium Putting Nexus Programming into Action
Abstract: This report documents the experience of the Nexus Platform — a consortium of eight Somali NGOs (CPD, GREDO, HAVOYOCO, KAALO, SSWC, SADO, TASCO, WASDA) alongside Oxfam and Save the Children International — in operationalising Triple Nexus programming in Somalia and Somaliland. Title: Envisioning the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in the Rohingya Response in Bangladesh: Implementation Challenges and Suggestions for the Future
Abstract:
The article focuses on the implementation challenges of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus in the Rohingya humanitarian response in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. It discusses the reliance of over a million Rohingya refugees on humanitarian aid since 2017 and identifies five main challenges hindering the HDP nexus approach. These include the undefined 'peace' component, dominance of international organizations undermining local capacities, ambiguities in multi-year funding, coordination gaps between the nexus pillars, and the reluctance of the Bangladesh government to design long-term refugee policies.

The article emphasizes the need for stronger political commitment from the Government of Bangladesh, effective national policy, and better integration of conflict-sensitive peace elements. It also provides insights for other forced migration and refugee crises globally, recommending collaboration, multi-year financing, and local capacity building to enhance the effectiveness of HDP nexus programming in crisis situations.

Title: Ethiopia's Nutrition Centric Triple Nexus Approach: A Summary
Abstract:
Ethiopia\'s Nutrition Centric Triple Nexus Approach addresses long-standing humanitarian challenges through a coordinated framework integrating humanitarian, development, and peace initiatives. Launched by the Government of Ethiopia (GoE) in May 2023, the approach aims to enhance community resilience, decrease malnutrition, and mitigate conflicts. The Implementation Roadmap outlines three phases: inception (2023-2024), implementation (2025-2029), and dissemination (from 2030). Key goals include reducing child stunting, improving dietary diversity, and fostering local peacebuilding. Governance is centered around the Food System and Nutrition Council (FSNC) with oversight by various ministries.

The operational guide outlines requirements for Nexus compliance, such as joint assessments, multi-year financing, and conflict sensitivity. The initial roll-out targets six woredas in crisis-prone regions, with a three-year budget estimated at US\$27 million. Emphasis is placed on flexible financing, multi-sectoral collaboration, and local empowerment. The approach advocates for systemic changes in financing and governance strategies to sustainably address Ethiopia\'s nutrition and conflict challenges.

Title: Evaluation of FAO's Contribution to the Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus 2014–2020
Abstract:
This FAO external evaluation (2021) reviews how FAO addressed the HDP nexus across its operations from 2014 to 2020, bringing together in a coherent narrative FAO's approaches to conflict management, peace-sustaining work on natural resources, rights-based frameworks, and emergency activities in crisis and conflict contexts. 

The evaluation finds that FAO's nexus contribution has been primarily at country level and draws on examples from across FAO's portfolio to generate lessons. The overarching finding is that FAO is ideally placed to mainstream and institutionalise HDP nexus ways of working as part of its organisational DNA, with specific recommendations on conflict-sensitive programming, technical diplomacy, joint analysis, and coordination. Title: Evaluation of IOM's Institutional Approach to the Implementation of the Humanitarian Development Peace Nexus
Abstract:
This evaluation examines the International Organization for Migration (IOM)'s institutional approach to the Humanitarian Development Peace Nexus (HDPN). It assesses IOM's strategic and operational integration of the HDPN framework across various contexts. The evaluation finds that while IOM has progressed in aligning with global HDPN strategies, internal challenges such as siloed operations, limited funding streams, and inconsistent field-level application persist. 

Key dimensions of operationalization, such as planning, assessment, programming, and partnerships, have shown varied effectiveness. There is a need for enhanced internal coherence, sustainable funding, integrated programming, and strengthened partnerships, especially with local actors. Recommendations include issuing high-level institutional guidance, fostering integrated programming, enhancing M&E frameworks, and prioritizing strategic donor engagement.

The report underscores the importance of coherent leadership and systemic approaches to ensure HDPN becomes a more effective and sustainable framework within IOM\'s operations.

Abstract:

It highlights UNDP\'s contributions to stabilizing, building, and strengthening institutions while enabling statebuilding and peacebuilding processes across diverse conflict contexts.

The report acknowledges UNDP's agility in adapting to various conflict situations and effectiveness in its interventions regarding recovery and stabilization. However, it notes areas for improvement, such as the need for a more proactive approach to conflict prevention, long-term engagement in governance, and private sector development.

The report stresses the necessity for integrated humanitarian-development-peace nexus programming, and the importance of addressing gender equality and enhancing youth roles in peacebuilding. Title: Evaluation of UNDP Support to Social Protection
Abstract:
The UNDP evaluation on social protection highlights its role in addressing social protection gaps through strengthening governance and systems to reach vulnerable populations. It acknowledges challenges in coverage, financing, among others, exacerbated by COVID-19.

The evaluation underscores the importance of leveraging UNDP's multisectoral approach to link social protection with governance, inclusive growth and environmental sustainability, while noting that programming is often fragmented and inconsistent.

Major contributions include targeting beneficiaries for cash transfers, building digital registries, and supporting health systems, but interventions remain limited in low-income countries. Title: Evaluation of UNDP Support to the Syrian Refugee Crisis Response
Abstract:
The evaluation by the UNDP Independent Evaluation Office scrutinizes the UNDP's response to the Syrian refugee crisis over 2015-2019. It underscores the importance of an integrated resilience approach combining humanitarian aid with long-term development goals amid this protracted crisis. 

The UNDP coordinated the 3RP framework alongside UNHCR to simultaneously address refugee and host communities' needs, achieving significant successes in mobilizing resources. Nevertheless, challenges persist in bridging the humanitarian-development divide due to constraints in institutional capacity and policy-level engagement.

The implementation of resilience strategies revealed limitations in achieving large-scale employment and adequately strengthening social services. Collaborative efforts with national and local governments proved essential in improving infrastructures and livelihoods, though heightened focus on private sector engagement was found lacking.

The evaluation stresses the urgent need for a strategic and coherent refugee response, balancing immediate humanitarian needs with sustainable development. It encourages leveraging UNDP\'s role in fostering long-term peace and development through multi-stakeholder partnerships and institutional strengthening.

Title: Evidence base for EU action on fragility and HDP nexus
Abstract:
This VOICE paper synthesises the available evidence base for EU action on fragility and the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, providing a critical assessment of what the research tells us about what works, what doesn't, and where the evidence is weak.

As the EU has made the HDP nexus central to its external action in fragile and conflict-affected states — through the 2017 Integrated Approach, the EU Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI-Global Europe), and successor financing frameworks — the quality and strength of the evidence base underpinning its nexus commitments is essential. 

The paper reviews evidence from evaluations, academic research, and grey literature on EU nexus implementation across pilot countries, examining where coherence and complementarity across the EU's humanitarian, development and political instruments have been achieved and where significant gaps remain. It makes evidence-based recommendations for how the EU can strengthen its nexus approach, particularly in relation to civil society engagement, humanitarian principles, and the quality of contextual analysis.

Abstract:
The paper explores the integration of peace within the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDPN), emphasizing the need for simultaneous and collaborative approaches to crises such as conflicts, disasters, and socio-economic shocks. Title: Falling short? Humanitarian funding and reform
Abstract:
The report 'Falling Short? Humanitarian Funding and Reform' critically analyzes the current state and future of humanitarian financing, emphasizing funding challenges and reform efforts amidst increasing global humanitarian needs. Despite historic levels of international humanitarian assistance, a significant funding gap of USD 32 billion was recorded in 2023. The trend shows declining donor contributions, with significant cuts from major donors like the UK, Germany, and Canada, while a narrowing donor base raises concerns about financial sustainability.

The report highlights the lack of substantial progress in directing resources to local and national actors, with only 4.4% of funding reaching them directly. Additionally, while cash and voucher assistance (CVA) has grown, its adoption in humanitarian settings has stalled, indicating a need for more localized approaches. Funding for anticipatory action remains limited, making up less than 1% of total international humanitarian assistance, signaling the need for more investment in anticipatory frameworks.

The overarching challenge remains the protracted nature of crises, which now account for 91% of global funding needs, prompting a call for multi-year funding approaches and connection with the humanitarian-development-peace nexus.

Title: FAO Guide to Context Analysis: Informing FAO Decision-Making – Approaches to Working in Fragile and Conflict-Affected Contexts
Abstract:
In 2018 FAO approved its Corporate Framework to Support Sustainable Peace in the Context of Agenda 2030, committing FAO to a more deliberate and transformative impact on sustaining peace, within the scope of its mandate. The foundational element for FAO supported interventions to - at a minimum - do no harm, or to identify where they may contribute to sustaining peace, is to understand contextual dynamics and how they could interact with a proposed intervention. This is essential to effective conflict-sensitive programming. The Guide to Context Analysis is a key step in operationalising this, being an accessible and practical learning tool for non-conflict specialists in FAO decentralised offices to document and institutionalise their knowledge of the local context, and thus inform conflict-sensitive design of FAO interventions.

The wider objective is to minimise the risk of any negative or harmful impacts, as well as maximise any positive contributions towards strengthening and consolidating conditions for sustainable local peace. The Guide to Context Analysis is sufficiently flexible to suit a variety of potential audiences or reporting formats, including a rapid context analysis for a specific project, an area-based intervention, joint programming with other UN agencies, as well as a standalone strategic analysis to inform decentralised office planning. The Guide can be read both a standalone instructional aid on context analysis, as well as an essential precursor to FAO’s Programme Clinic approach to design conflict-sensitive interventions (comprising both a facilitators’ and participants’ guides).

Title: Financing Food Security: Promises and Pitfalls of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in South Sudan
Abstract:
This SIPRI policy report explores the potential for donor governments and institutions to support operationalisation of the HDP nexus to address South Sudan's severe food insecurity crisis, where 70% of the population is severely food insecure despite nearly $13 billion in ODA since independence in 2011. 

The study finds that despite commitments to work across the HDP nexus, donor financing remains largely siloed in separate humanitarian, development and peacebuilding funding streams. It examines donors' perspectives on HDP nexus financing approaches to food security, identifies structural constraints — including inflexible funding cycles, short programming horizons, and risk aversion — and proposes ways forward for ensuring food security through better-integrated financing.

Title: Financing Food Security: Promises And Pitfalls of The Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus In South Sudan
Abstract:
This study explores the potential for donor governments and institutions to support the operationalization of the humanitarian, development
and peacebuilding (HDP) nexus to respond to the food insecurity crisis in South Sudan and the challenges it presents.

South Sudan faces one of the worst hunger crises in the world. Violent conflict, climate shocks and widespread economic crisis have left 70 per cent of the population severely food insecure. Donors have provided nearly $13 billion in official development assistance (ODA) since the country’s independence in 2011, of which a large proportion has been allocated to the food security sector, but the number of food insecure people is higher than ever.

Despite commitments to work across the HDP nexus, donor financing remains largely siloed in humanitarian, development and peacebuilding funding streams. Almost all the ODA provided is earmarked, which prevents much-needed collaboration among implementing actors and limits the ability to pool resources and adapt to ever-changing conflict and peacebuilding dynamics.

Title: Financing for stability
Abstract:
This OECD Policy Paper, 'Financing for Stability,' provides guidelines for developing financing strategies in fragile contexts. It underscores the necessity of new financing approaches to address the complexities of the Agenda 2030 goals, particularly within contexts that require both urgent humanitarian aid and long-term development investment. The guidance emphasizes the importance of a coordinated strategy that includes diverse actors and financing sources, advocating for a shift from funding to financing for sustainable results.

Key elements of the strategy involve understanding the current financial landscape, assessing and forecasting needs, matching appropriate financing tools, and developing resources mobilization plans. Importantly, it stresses adaptive governance and coordination mechanisms, with an emphasis on leveraging private sector investments and fostering national leadership.

The document identifies critical challenges such as overcoming fragmentation in donor approaches and prioritizing actions that have significant impacts on stability and growth. Additionally, the paper recommends practical steps and the importance of risk-informed planning to enhance resilience.

Title: Financing fragile contexts: What can development finance institutions do better?
Abstract:
The paper explores how development finance institutions (DFIs) invest in fragile and conflict-affected countries (FCACs). Currently, FCACs are lagging in achieving Sustainable Development Goals due to fragility, conflict, poor governance, and weak macroeconomic conditions.

Although official development assistance is the primary external financing for FCACs, DFIs are crucial for driving private sector development and economic recovery. DFIs confront challenges such as high transaction costs, political and financial risks, and inadequate expertise, limiting their effectiveness in FCACs.

Recommendations include adopting conflict sensitivity strategies, improving the investment climate, developing specific mandates for FCACs, and utilizing blended finance approaches. The paper advocates for strategic partnerships, enhanced expertise, and joint efforts to build resilient markets and facilitate socio-economic development in FCACs.

Title: Financing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:
The briefing from the Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office highlights the role of pooled funds in bridging the humanitarian-development-peace nexus. These flexible financial instruments are essential for addressing protracted crises, which result in increased humanitarian needs and challenges to achieving Sustainable Development Goals in volatile settings.

The document discusses the creation and significance of pooled funding mechanisms that blend, sequence, and combine financial resources across crisis-affected countries. It emphasizes the benefits of pooled funds, including improved efficiency, risk management, and collective outcomes. Examples like the South Sudan Multi-Partner Trust Fund and the UN Post-Conflict MPTF for Colombia showcase successful applications. Innovations such as the Humanitarian Window of the Malawi One Fund illustrate the ability of pooled funds to swiftly respond to emergencies and coordinate effective interventions.

The office aims to refine these funding instruments to better support the humanitarian-development-peace nexus with enhanced flexibility and coherence for future interventions.

Title: Financing the Nexus - Gaps and opportunities from a field perspective
Abstract:
The report 'Financing the Nexus - Gaps and opportunities from a field perspective' investigates the availability and role of predictable, multi-year, flexible financing to support humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding efforts (the 'triple nexus') in crisis-affected settings. It studies the alignment of funding with collective outcomes in humanitarian and development strategies, based on case studies of Cameroon, Central African Republic (CAR), Chad, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and Ukraine. Despite political support, practical application is unclear due to non-adapted funding tools, mixed government engagement, and coordination challenges.

The report highlights the rise of multilateral development banks and new financing instruments, but identifies issues with transparency, policy coherence, and insufficient engagement from bilateral donors. Recommendations include defining the nexus scope, enhancing coordination, addressing donor disincentives, ensuring strategic and flexible financing, and improving institutional capabilities for better programming.

Title: Flagship Initiative First Year Learning Report
Abstract:
The Flagship Initiative (FI) represents a reform effort aimed at centralizing and responding to the priorities of affected communities in humanitarian settings, with pilot projects in Niger, South Sudan, Philippines, and Colombia. In its first year, the FI focused on community engagement and decentralized coordination, highlighting an existing gap in aligning humanitarian responses with community needs. 

Key insights suggest transactional community interactions currently dominate humanitarian processes, which do not prioritize or incorporate community capacities effectively. Each country advanced unique tools for community engagement and area-based coordination, allowing for varied learning opportunities. 

The document underscores the challenge of harmonizing qualitative community data with traditional, quantitative needs assessments and advocates for improved integration to enable responsive programming. Financing models, including country-based pooled funds, showed potential but remained traditional, with emphasis needed on supporting local actors and aligning funds with community-driven priorities. In its next phase, the FI aims to focus on scaling best practices, fostering sub-national presence, and ensuring programming reflects community needs, bolstered by flexible financial support strategies.

Title: Forcibly Displaced: Toward a Development Approach Supporting Refugees, the Internally Displaced, and Their Hosts
Abstract:
This World Bank report, produced in close partnership with UNHCR, argues that forced displacement must be understood and addressed as a development challenge — not solely a humanitarian one. With over 65 million forcibly displaced persons at time of publication, 95% in developing countries and over half displaced for more than four years, the report advocates for a development approach that complements humanitarian emergency response. It focuses on addressing medium- and long-term socioeconomic challenges — employment, education, social cohesion, gender equity — for both the displaced and their host communities.

The report identifies four core dimensions: addressing specific vulnerabilities of the displaced, supporting host communities, maintaining a medium-to-long-term perspective, and building broad partnerships.

Title: Formative Evaluation of the Integration by UNDP of the Principles of Leaving No One Behind
Abstract:
This report evaluates the integration of the 'Leave No One Behind' (LNOB) principles within the UNDP\'s programs and operations. It highlights the significance of the LNOB and Reaching the Furthest Behind First (RFBF) commitments in addressing global inequality and poverty. 

The evaluation covers UNDP's strategic positioning, effectiveness, and programmatic performance from 2018 to mid-2022 across its Signature Solutions: poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality. It finds that UNDP has made contributions to conceptual clarity and data analytics for inequality, strengthening governance structures, climate adaptation programming, and energy access.

However, there is a need to prioritize reaching the furthest behind and operationalize LNOB in a more coherent manner with clearer guidance and resources. Recommendations include adopting an 'equality+' promise, building strategic leadership on LNOB/RFBF, fostering partnerships with non-governmental actors, and ensuring better financing strategies to support LNOB initiatives.

Title: Formative evaluation of UNICEF work to link humanitarian and development programming
Abstract:
This formative evaluation by UNICEF assesses efforts to link humanitarian and development programming (LHD), giving insights and recommendations for improvements. The organization's advancements include notable progress through the 2019 mandatory Procedure on Linking Humanitarian and Development Programming and the revision of Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action in 2020. However, inconsistencies remain in understanding and implementing the Procedure across the organization.

The evaluation examines the policy coherence, partnership roles, planning and programming processes, internal systems and structures, and the impact of COVID-19 on nexus approaches. It calls for better integration of peacebuilding efforts and enhanced staff capacity in nexus areas. It also highlights the need for improved systems for monitoring, funding, and reporting nexus efforts to ensure efficient and consistent implementation across UNICEF's global programming.

Title: Fragile and Conflict-Affected Situations and Small Island Developing States Approach
Abstract:
The report outlines the Asian Development Bank's (ADB) approach to address the unique challenges faced by fragile and conflict-affected situations (FCAS) and small island developing states (SIDS). These regions have distinct issues such as governance deficits, geographic isolation, small populations, narrow asset bases, and sometimes armed conflict or other fragilities including climate change.

The FCAS and SIDS approach (FSA) involves flexible and tailored interventions aiming to improve governance, strengthen project implementation, and build resilience in these areas. The strategy emphasizes risk-informed decision-making, improved classification criteria, enhanced institutional capacity, and strategic partnerships. It aims to better coordinate ADB\'s resources and build on lessons learned from previous plans and operations.

The approach integrates factors like fragility and resilience into project cycles, promoting inclusive and responsive strategies to ensure sustainable development outcomes.

Title: Fragility and displacement: a people-centred approach to working across the nexus
Abstract:
This VOICE paper makes the case for a fundamentally people-centred approach to the humanitarian-development-peace nexus in contexts of fragility and displacement. It argues that much nexus programming remains system- and institution-focused — oriented around coordination mechanisms, collective outcomes, and donor frameworks — rather than genuinely centred on the rights, agency, and priorities of displaced and crisis-affected people.

Drawing on evidence from multiple fragile contexts, the paper identifies what a people-centred nexus approach requires in practice: meaningful participation of affected populations in decision-making, accountability mechanisms that work for communities rather than donors, and programming that starts from the assets and capacities of displaced people rather than treating them as passive recipients.

It makes concrete recommendations for NGOs, UN agencies, and bilateral donors on redesigning nexus approaches around people's real needs and lived experiences.

Title: Fragility Risk and Resilience Analysis Tool (FRAAT)
Abstract:
The Fragility Risk and Resilience Analysis Tool (FRRAT) is designed to facilitate the evaluation of fragility risks and resilience systems in countries where Denmark is actively engaged, especially in the contexts of the Humanitarian-Development-Peacebuilding (HDP) Nexus.

The tool is informed by the OECD/DAC framework and consists of two matrices which enable teams to conduct comprehensive analyses of mult-dimensional fragility risks across five spheres: political, economic, societal, environmental, and security. Matrix 1 addresses 'problem-side' analysis focusing on the various stresses and risks contributing to fragility, while Matrix 2 combines this with 'solution-focused' analyses of coping capacities and resilience systems, thus guiding strategic decisions for Danish engagement.

The tool emphasizes secondary source utilization and collaborative team sessions to synthesize insights efficiently, integrating considerations like the Women Peace and Security agenda, climate variability risks, forced displacement, and migration aspects. FRRAT supports anticipatory decision-making and aims to enhance collaboration and effectiveness in Danish engagements across priority countries.

Title: Framework For Conflict-Sensitive Programming In Iraq
Abstract:
The Framework for Conflict-Sensitive Programming in Iraq report, drafted by various UN agencies and NGOs under UNHCR coordination, aims to address Iraq's pervasive violence from multiple dimensions. The report engages in a detailed analysis of Iraq's complex conflict dynamics, encompassing sectarian violence, insurgency, counter-insurgency, organized crime, and domestic violence. It highlights the causes such as political vacuums and weak law enforcement and explores the roles of 'conflict promoters' alongside 'peacemakers,' including civil society players and religious figures.

The report suggests integrating conflict management into aid and development efforts, emphasizing a need for 'Do No Harm' principles and the reformation of structural approaches to humanitarian aid to mitigate further conflict. Additionally, it calls for increased funding and the incorporation of existing peace mechanisms into programming. The report recommends mainstreaming conflict management activities within developmental initiatives to avoid exacerbating existing intergroup tensions and promote reconciliation.

Title: Framework for Health in the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Africa
Abstract:
This WHO framework publication (2024) provides comprehensive guidance for operationalising health in the HDP nexus in African countries with fragile, conflict and violence (FCV) contexts. Developed jointly with the African Union Commission, it is described as the first of its kind globally to guide health policy and planning across the nexus.

The framework defines cross-cutting areas of change and guiding principles; outlines roles of governments, WHO, the African Union, regional economic communities, and bilateral and multilateral partners; and provides recommendations for operationalisation with the goal of attaining collective health outcomes.

Key areas include health sector development planning, budgeting, intersectoral coordination, services delivery, and monitoring. Designed to accelerate translation of the HDPN approach into practice in Africa and beyond.

Title: French-German development collaboration in MENA: Options for humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) and triple nexus cooperation in Libya and Iraq
Abstract:
This German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) Discussion Paper examines the potential for enhanced French-German development cooperation in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region specifically through the humanitarian-development-peace nexus framework. France and Germany are among the largest bilateral donors active in the MENA region, where protracted conflicts in Syria, Yemen, Libya, and Iraq have generated massive humanitarian needs alongside major development financing requirements.

The paper analyses existing French-German collaboration modalities, identifies where their respective comparative advantages — in humanitarian assistance, development cooperation, and political engagement — could be better aligned through a nexus approach, and explores specific options for joint programming, co-financing mechanisms, and coordinated political engagement.

It makes concrete recommendations for how the two countries could strengthen their bilateral nexus collaboration in MENA as a model for broader European donor coordination in fragile contexts.

Title: From Concept to Practice: The Rise and Uncertainty of the Triple Nexus Approach
Abstract:
Chapter 6 of the Global Policy triple nexus e-book series, this contribution by Ferrero Baselga and Mena features a rich conversation with Dr. Sylvia Brown, a practitioner with extensive experience thinking, implementing, and evaluating triple nexus projects across multiple organisations. The chapter traces the evolution of the triple nexus from its conceptual origins at the World Humanitarian Summit through to current uncertainties about its viability under changing political tides.

Brown discusses the structural challenge of the peace pillar — where no single actor has taken clear responsibility — and examines how organisations like Oxfam have developed their own understanding of 'positive peace' to drive nexus implementation. She argues that, despite the funding gap and systemic obstacles, country office demand for the nexus remains strong, and organisations must adapt it to new contexts including climate programming.

Title: From Emergency Relief to Development Holds: The Developmental Shift in the ICRC's Humanitarian Assistance in Protracted Conflict
Abstract:
Published in the Journal of Conflict and Security Law (Oxford Academic, 2025), this legal-academic article examines the developmental shift in ICRC humanitarian assistance from a novel legal perspective. It analyses how the ICRC's mandate and operations have expanded over time beyond emergency relief — to essential services, infrastructure rebuilding, livelihood support, and institutional capacity building — in response to protracted conflict settings where the traditional relief-development binary breaks down.

The article traces the evolution of the World Bank-ICRC partnership through successive MOUs and Operational Framework Agreements, including the 2024 renewal, and examines how this institutional shift is reshaping the legal frameworks governing humanitarian action. Essential reading for scholars and senior practitioners interested in how the ICRC navigates the nexus between humanitarian principles and developmental programming.

Title: From Protracted Conflict to Sustainable Peace? The Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus and International Law
Abstract:
This Oxford University Press academic book provides a comprehensive scholarly examination of the humanitarian-development-peace nexus as a framework for responding to protracted conflicts and supporting transitions towards sustainable peace.

Bringing together contributions from leading scholars and practitioners, the book interrogates the theoretical foundations, political economy, and operational realities of the triple nexus in diverse conflict and post-conflict contexts. It examines the intellectual genealogy of nexus thinking — tracing its roots through LRRD, resilience, early recovery, and previous relief-development debates — and assesses the extent to which the current HDP nexus framework represents a genuine conceptual and operational advance. Individual chapters examine nexus implementation across different sectors and contexts, critically assess its political assumptions, and explore the structural tensions between humanitarian principles, development effectiveness, and political peacebuilding.

The book provides an essential scholarly reference for academics, advanced students, and sophisticated practitioners seeking to understand the nexus at depth.

Title: From Silos to Synergies: Partnering for Social Cohesion in the Sahel
Abstract:
This SIPRI Policy Paper examines how international actors can move from siloed approaches to genuine synergies in supporting social cohesion in the Sahel — one of the world's most complex and deteriorating humanitarian-development-peace contexts.

Social cohesion — understood as the capacity of communities and societies to manage their differences peacefully, maintain trust, and cooperate across ethnic, religious, and political lines — is increasingly recognised as both a prerequisite for and an outcome of effective HDP nexus programming in the Sahel.

The paper analyses why social cohesion programming has often been fragmented across humanitarian, development and peace actors in the Sahel, with each sector pursuing distinct approaches with limited coordination. It examines specific partnership models that have enabled more synergistic action, including examples from Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, and Chad, and draws lessons on the enabling conditions — including flexible financing, adaptive programming, and genuine local partnership — that make synergistic social cohesion programming possible.

Title: Funding Cuts and Nexus Thinking: What Can Aid Actors Learn from the 'Beautiful Game'?
Abstract:
This ODI think piece uses the metaphor of football to interrogate current approaches to the humanitarian-development-peace nexus and why they fall short. Written against the backdrop of record aid funding cuts in 2025, it argues that the relay race model of nexus — where the baton passes sequentially from humanitarian to development to peace actors — is unhelpful in fragile and conflict-affected settings where all three must act simultaneously. 

Drawing on the analogy of team sports, it calls for a shift from sectoral thinking to genuine teamwork: coordination that respects operational boundaries while pursuing complementarity. It also argues that local voices and actors must be brought to the centre of nexus thinking, as they already work holistically across the full HDP range of needs without the silos that constrain international actors.

Title: Gender equality across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace nexus
Abstract:
This OECD paper discusses the integration of gender equality within the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus. It highlights the importance of addressing gender inequalities, which are drivers of vulnerabilities and fragility.

The paper reviews selected Development Assistance Committee members' strategies, revealing that gender equality is widely reflected but needs further emphasis. It advocates for gender-sensitive analysis, the incorporation of women into peace processes, and consideration of the role of masculinities. Increased attention to gender is linked to strengthening coherence across the nexus, supporting women's empowerment, and addressing gender-based violence.

The paper urges better collaboration, analysis, and practical guidance, emphasizing the 'do no harm' principle in nexus approaches for SEAH prevention and response.

Title: Give 'P' a Chance: Peacebuilding, Peace Operations and the HDP Nexus
Abstract: This report by the Center for International Peace Operations (ZIF) and the German Development Cooperation (GIZ) examines how peacebuilding and peace operations actors can be better integrated into HDP Nexus frameworks. It argues that the 'P' — peace — dimension of the nexus is consistently underdeveloped, poorly resourced, and operationally fragmented. The paper analyses the structural and institutional reasons for this marginalisation, examines how peace operations and peacebuilding actors can bring comparative advantages, and proposes concrete recommendations for better integration of peace in joint analysis, programming, and financing across the HDP Nexus.

Title: Glimmers of Confidence in Pibor, South Sudan — Where the Triple Nexus Grows Unscripted
Abstract:
Chapter 10 of the Global Policy triple nexus e-book series, this practitioner contribution from Van Hall Larenstein University examines how the triple nexus manifests spontaneously and organically in the everyday lives of communities and local NGOs in Pibor, South Sudan — without being explicitly labelled or planned as such. Drawing on field experience with Help a Child and local partners, the author argues that international actors often fail to recognise that local solidarity mechanisms already embody nexus logic, and that labelling and framing by international actors can distort rather than support these organic processes. 

The piece shows how linking humanitarian, development, and peace approaches naturally occurs through local actors' strategies to address their struggles, offering important lessons for how international nexus programming should learn from and build on local practice rather than imposing external frameworks.

Title: Global Collaboration Framework for Inclusion and Solutions 2023-2025
Abstract:
The UNDP-UNHCR Global Collaboration Framework for Inclusion and Solutions 2023-2025 aims to address the growing challenges of forced displacement and statelessness exacerbated by conflicts, climate change, and other global crises. It emphasizes the need for combined humanitarian and development actions along with peacebuilding efforts to foster stability and sustainable solutions.

The framework builds on previous collaborative efforts and targets seven areas: livelihoods, SDG integration, rule of law/local governance, conflict prevention/peacebuilding, climate change/environment, internal displacement, and statelessness. By leveraging the comparative advantages of UNDP and UNHCR, the framework seeks to boost development financing, technical assistance, and advocacy to support displaced populations and host communities. It advocates for inclusive growth, gender equality, and sustainable resource management in displacement settings, with a focus on policy integration, capacity building, and joint resource mobilization at both regional and country levels.

Title: Global Compact on Refugees
Abstract: The Global Compact on Refugees, adopted by the UN General Assembly in December 2018, provides a framework for more equitable and predictable burden- and responsibility-sharing among states for large refugee movements and protracted situations. Informed by the 1951 Refugee Convention and grounded in international law, the Compact establishes four objectives: ease pressures on host countries; enhance refugee self-reliance; expand access to third-country solutions; and support conditions for return in safety and dignity. It calls for a 'whole-of-society' approach and increased development actor engagement, making it a key policy anchor for HDP Nexus approaches in displacement contexts.

Title: Global Humanitarian Assistance Report 2025
Abstract:
The 2025 Global Humanitarian Assistance (GHA) Report — the world-leading annual assessment of international humanitarian financing, now produced by ALNAP (formerly by Development Initiatives) — documents the largest-ever recorded fall in humanitarian funding. International humanitarian assistance declined by almost USD 5 billion (10%) in 2024, and scenarios suggest government donor funding could drop between 34% and 45% by end-2025 compared to the 2023 peak.

A dedicated chapter analyses the shifting 'tectonic plates' of broader crisis financing across the HDP nexus and climate, revealing that peace funding in protracted HRP contexts has reached historic lows as a share of ODA — directly contrary to the aims of the OECD DAC Recommendation. Essential reading for any practitioner engaging with nexus financing arguments.

Abstract:

The strategy advocates for coordinated efforts across humanitarian, development, and peace sectors to achieve collective outcomes that align with the 2030 Agenda.

The approach calls for enhanced partnerships, comprehensive planning, and recalibration of funding mechanisms. The Global WASH Cluster (GWC) is pivotal in driving these collaborative efforts with a focus on resilience, conflict sensitivity, and peacebuilding.

Title: Good Practice Guide for HDP Nexus Operationalisation
Abstract:
This practical guide from BICC (Bonn International Centre for Conflict Studies) compiles evidence-based good practices for operationalising the humanitarian-development-peace nexus at the country and programme level.

Drawing on extensive field research conducted across multiple fragile and conflict-affected contexts — including Mali, Iraq, South Sudan and others — the guide distils lessons from both successful and unsuccessful nexus implementation efforts. It covers the full programme cycle from joint situation analysis through to planning, implementation, monitoring and learning, with a particular focus on locally-led peace, gender dynamics, and the specific challenge of integrating the peace dimension meaningfully rather than treating it as an afterthought. 

The guide addresses structural enablers and barriers including coordination mechanisms, financing architecture, and organisational mandates, and provides concrete, actionable recommendations for practitioners, coordination bodies, and donors seeking to advance genuine nexus coherence rather than mere rhetorical alignment.

Title: Good practices in the operationalisation of the humanitarian-developmentpeace nexus
Abstract:
This guide provides practical recommendations for implementing the humanitarian-development-peace nexus within EU external action, specifically through the Team Europe Approach. It draws on field experiences from six EU pilot countries: Chad, Iraq, Myanmar, Nigeria, Sudan, and Uganda, and other fragile contexts. Key practices include strengthening coordination among actors, conducting joint analyses to understand conflict drivers, and developing integrated programs to enhance resilience. It emphasizes the importance of supporting peace-building efforts in conflict areas and ensuring sufficient funding for risk-reducing activities.

The guide also encourages developing 'soft' security strategies to address instability and complex crises. Specific financing mechanisms are recommended to support hybrid actions transcending traditional humanitarian and development boundaries. Additionally, joint monitoring and evaluation are highlighted to improve ongoing interventions and contribute to collective learning and sharing. These practices aim to address root causes of crises, enhance the operationalization of the nexus, and build long-term community resilience.

Title: Governing Complexity in Complex Times: The HDP Nexus and the Role of the UN, the EU and the World Bank
Abstract:
This journal article analyzes the Nexus-based approach of the United Nations, European Union, and World Bank in addressing complex humanitarian-development-security crises through coordinated efforts. The Triple Nexus concept is explored for its potential in experimentalist governance, showcasing increased institutional cooperation but highlighting ongoing challenges, particularly with peacebuilding integration.

Case studies of Cameroon, Myanmar, and the Democratic Republic of Congo demonstrate varied success in Nexus implementation, emphasizing the need for local community empowerment and more comprehensive coordination amongst donors. Despite improved dialogue, the article identifies persistent hurdles, such as the peace dimension, in ensuring inclusive, rights-based governance. Future progress relies heavily on enhancing bottom-up components and diplomatic engagement for sustainable development and conflict resolution.

Title: Guidelines for integrating gender-based violence interventions in humanitarian action
Abstract:
These guidelines provide practical guidance and effective tools for humanitarians and communities affected by armed conflict, natural disasters and other humanitarian emergencies to coordinate, plan, implement, monitor and evaluate essential actions for the prevention and mitigation of gender-based violence (GBV), accross all stages of disaster and emergency management: from preparedness to recovery.

The document outlines how, in order to save lives and maximize protection, essential actions must be undertaken in a coordinated manner from the earliest stages of emergency preparedness.

These actions are necessary in every humanitarian crisis and are focused on three overarching and interlinked goals described in this document: 

1. To reduce risk of GBV by implementing GBV prevention and mitigation strategies across all areas of humanitarian response from pre-emergency through to recovery stages;
2. To promote resilience by strengthening national and community-based systems that prevent and mitigate GBV, and by enabling survivors and those at risk of GBV to access care and support; and
3. To aid recovery of communities and societies by supporting local and national capacity to create lasting solutions to the problem of GBV.

Title: Guidelines on the Humanitarian, Development and Peace Nexus
Abstract:
Official guidelines (MAECI-DGCS and AICS, 2023) setting out the strategic approach and operational methods through which the Italian development cooperation system implements the HDP Nexus in fragile and protracted crisis contexts. Developed through a working group involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS), civil society organisations and universities, the guidelines operationalise the 2019 OECD DAC Recommendation within Italy's domestic legal framework (Law 125/2014). 

They define how the Italian system approaches coordination (joint context analysis, collective outcomes, pilot fragile country processes), programming (joined-up planning across the three pillars using comparative advantages), and financing (evidence-based, multi-annual, flexible instruments including pooled funds and innovative financing). Includes the full text of the 2019 OECD DAC Recommendation as an annex. An important example of a bilateral donor translating the DAC Recommendation into a nationally-specific operational framework.

This guidance translates that commitment into operational practice, explaining how WASH cluster coordinators can help bridge humanitarian response with longer-term WASH development goals, promote joint analysis and joint planning across the three nexus pillars, and contribute to sustainable, resilience-oriented WASH outcomes.

Title: HDP Nexus and Conflict Sensitivity: Changing the Aid System for Good?
Abstract:
This swisspeace 'Essential' publication examines the synergies and overlaps between the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus and conflict sensitivity approaches, arguing that both share underlying objectives of improving aid effectiveness in conflict-affected contexts. 

The paper contends that while conflict sensitivity has been implemented in a minimalist way and the HDP Nexus remains largely conceptual, together they can produce transformative change. It identifies key overlapping dimensions including: context as the starting point, community engagement, transfer of power to the local level, adaptability, and coordination.

The paper concludes that both approaches must be adopted as genuine mindsets rather than institutional tick-boxes to meaningfully reform the aid system.

Title: HDP Nexus Implementation in South Sudan — Localisation from a Decolonial Perspective
Abstract:
This BICC Spotlight Paper (2024) provides in-depth analysis of the HDP nexus in South Sudan from a decolonial perspective. It is one of three country spotlights accompanying the broader BICC Discussion Paper on bottom-up nexus implementation. Key findings show that the HDP nexus in South Sudan emerged as a top-down process, driven by the UN system in collaboration with the transitional government, raising questions of accountability and local ownership.

The paper examines how localisation has largely been interpreted as a resource shift to national and local NGOs, without substantively transforming power structures or decision-making processes. It highlights the need to rethink localisation through a decolonial lens — ensuring that communities are genuinely centred and that power imbalances within the aid system are confronted rather than reproduced.

Title: HDP Nexus: Challenges and Opportunities for its Implementation
Abstract:
The report evaluates the implementation of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (Triple Nexus) commissioned by the European Commission. It assesses processes across nine countries, revealing significant understanding of the Nexus\'s value in managing protracted crises. Despite this, operational challenges such as resource gaps, bureaucratic burdens, and conflicting institutional mandates persist.

The integration of peace within the Nexus presents complexities, potentially undermining humanitarian principles. Recommendations include promoting joint conflict analysis, employing flexible financing strategies, and enhancing leadership roles to drive Nexus implementation. Countries involved have shown varied engagement, with TEIs identified as opportunities for deeper EUMS involvement.

The Nexus supports transitioning from emergency interventions to sustainable service delivery, though monitoring progress remains challenging. Actions focusing on community resilience, social cohesion, and governance have been operationalized across sectors and geographical contexts, spotlighting the Nexus's flexibility yet complexity in diverse environments.

The NWOW demands active participation from national governments, local authorities, civil society, and bilateral and multilateral partners in a collaborative effort.

Principled humanitarian action was underscored as essential for life-saving responses. Participants identified key action areas including country-led effort support, flexible multi-year planning, and prioritizing prevention.

The NWOW also calls for improved financing mechanisms to enable outcomes that connect humanitarian response and development efforts. Key entities pledged commitments to focus on collective outcomes and to enhance collaboration and financing strategies.

Title: How Can the HDP Nexus Work from the Bottom Up? A Discussion Paper on Implementation Challenges from a Decolonial Perspective
Abstract:
This BICC Discussion Paper uses decolonial critique to examine how the HDP nexus works in theory and practice, drawing on empirical research in Iraq, Mali, and South Sudan. The authors — Müller-Koné, Meininghaus, Kemmerling, and Haidara — argue that the power imbalances central to decolonial analysis pose a particular challenge for the HDP nexus: while the approach claims to be bottom-up, in practice it reproduces existing hierarchies between international and local actors.

Based on around 180 interviews with NGO staff and community members, the paper finds that collective outcomes and localisation remain top-down processes driven by UN and international NGO frameworks. It calls for a decolonial rethinking that acknowledges colonial legacies shaping funding flows, staffing, decision-making, and norms within the aid sector. Title: How to Decolonise the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus?
Abstract:
The BICC policy brief examines the challenges of implementing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus from a decolonial perspective. Despite its aim to address conflicts sustainably by linking humanitarian, development, and peace activities, this approach has been largely top-down rather than bottom-up, especially in Iraq, Mali, and South Sudan. The critique focuses on how power imbalances hinder the HDP nexus's effectiveness, suggesting that existing structures perpetuate these disparities rather than overcome them.

The promise of localization, as part of the HDP nexus, risks reproducing power imbalances since local actors still have limited influence on decision-making. Additionally, peace activities are often politically sensitive and controversial, as seen in Mali\'s stabilization policies and Iraq's local opposition.

The paper argues for decolonial reform, emphasizing greater involvement and decision-making power for local actors, recognizing indigenous knowledge, and addressing the root causes of conflict more effectively.

Title: Humanitarian Action and Peacebuilding: Incompatible or Complementary?
Abstract:
This chapter explores the intersection of humanitarian action and peacebuilding, focusing on whether these efforts are incompatible or complementary. It highlights the evolving nature of humanitarian aid, founded on principles such as humanity and impartiality, which has been increasingly merged with development aid and political objectives, particularly in Africa.

The author presents case studies from South Sudan, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Mali, illustrating the challenges faced by humanitarian actors amidst peacekeeping missions with expanded mandates. These missions often blur lines between peacekeeping, state-building, and counterterrorism, impacting humanitarian organizations' neutrality and effectiveness.

The recommendations emphasize the necessity of distinguishing the roles and mandates of humanitarian aid from peacekeeping missions, advocating for the separation and depoliticization of humanitarian efforts to maintain impartiality, enhance independence through diversified funding, and ensure adequate space for humanitarian missions to operate effectively.

Title: Humanitarian Action and Sustaining Peace
Abstract:

Historically regarded as a short-term response, humanitarian action now demands integration with long-term development and peace efforts due to increasingly protracted crises and violent conflicts. The document highlights the need for principled humanitarian action that is neutral and impartial, yet interconnected with sustaining peace practices. Key insights include leveraging local actors and capacities, providing context-specific aid, and ensuring conflict-sensitive responses.

The report underscores that humanitarian action alone cannot achieve peace but contributes significantly to resilience and development, laying the groundwork for peacebuilding initiatives. It reveals the operational and policy challenges in bridging humanitarian action with development and peacebuilding, advocating for strategic and sustainable humanitarian efforts in complex emergencies.

Title: Humanitarian Innovative Financing in Fragile Settings: Taking Stock and Charting the Road Ahead
Abstract:
This ODI Policy Brief, commissioned by the ICRC and the Humanitarian Innovative Finance Hub, examines the potential of humanitarian innovative financing (HIF) to bridge the growing humanitarian funding gap in fragile and conflict-affected settings. Drawing on a review of over 50 key literature sources on HIF models, it assesses the added value of blended finance, debt swaps, results-based financing, insurance mechanisms, and other innovative instruments in humanitarian contexts.

The brief explores specific cases including the ICRC-World Bank water programme in DRC that leveraged USD 10 million in grants to catalyse USD 30 million in concessional finance, and the IRC-EBRD partnership on wastewater infrastructure in Jordan. It makes recommendations for scaling up HIF while maintaining humanitarian principles, and feeds directly into the Grand Bargain 3.0 Innovative Financing workstream.

Title: Humanitarian Programme Cycle (IASC)
Abstract:
The Humanitarian Programme Cycle (HPC) is an operational framework developed by the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) that sets out the sequence of actions to prepare for, plan, manage, deliver and monitor collective responses in non-refugee humanitarian emergencies that may or may not have required a system-wide scale-up activation. Its successful implementation depends on emergency preparedness, effective coordination between national and local authorities and humanitarian actors, and information management.

The model is driven by collectively owned evidence-based plans, direction by humanitarian country teams (HCTs) led by a humanitarian coordinator (HC), and accountability for results. Its process and tools focus on humanitarian actors working at national and subnational level in the field, not on external audiences.

Title: Humanitarian Protection in the Liptako-Gourma Region (2020–2022): Local Protection and Humanitarian Mechanisms — Summary Report
Abstract:
Summary report synthesising findings from a two-year research programme (2020–2022) on humanitarian protection in the Liptako-Gourma tri-border area of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger — the epicentre of the Sahel crisis since 2015. Conducted in collaboration with the Danish Refugee Council, LASDEL (Niger), Point Sud (Mali) and the Centre for Democratic Governance (Burkina Faso), the research examined the effectiveness of humanitarian protection programmes and their relationship with local protection systems.

Key findings address the links between community-based and international humanitarian protection mechanisms, threats and vulnerabilities facing affected populations, and how protection programming can be strengthened through better integration of local knowledge and structures.

Title: Humanitarian Response in Violent Conflict: A Toolbox of Conflict Sensitive Indicators
Abstract:
The document serves as a tool designed to integrate conflict sensitivity into humanitarian response programs. It highlights the importance of merging humanitarian efforts with peacebuilding principles to mitigate adverse effects on beneficiaries during periods of violent conflict.

Key areas emphasized include comprehensive evaluation, early warning systems, capacity building, and adherence to norms ensuring no harm is inflicted. The toolkit provides indicators to guide organizations in adapting their strategies according to dynamic conflict conditions, encouraging inclusive programming and coordination among agencies for sustainable peace and development.

It stresses the significance of continuous performance appraisal and stakeholder accountability. Examples from past programs and recommended practices for conflict-sensitive planning are included, promoting improved dignity, justice, and equality in affected communities.

Title: Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:
This guidance note by Sida focuses on enhancing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus in global, regional, and bilateral efforts. It highlights the growing concentration of poverty in areas affected by conflict and crises, predicting that by 2030, up to 80% of the world\'s extreme poor will reside in these contexts. The HDP Nexus approach aims to improve coordination, coherence, and complementarity among humanitarian, development, and peace actions to reduce needs, risks, and vulnerabilities and prevent crises and conflicts.

The document elaborates on the nexus framework, including the DAC Recommendation's 11 principles that guide collaborative actions to achieve sustainable development and collective outcomes. It emphasizes a people-centered, conflict-sensitive, and preventive approach, advocating for strengthened local capacities, flexible financing, and evidence-based programming.

The note also covers operational guidance for Sida to integrate nexus principles in its operations, involving coordinated analysis, dialogue, resource allocation, and adaptive management while ensuring humanitarian principles are upheld.

Title: Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus Approaches in Conflict and Disaster Settings
Abstract:
The evaluation outlines the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus approach, aimed at reducing humanitarian needs and addressing root causes by fostering collaboration among humanitarian, development, and peace initiatives in conflict and disaster settings.

The approach leverages coordination frameworks, partnerships, and innovative financing strategies, aiming to embed livelihoods in humanitarian programs and overcome funding silos. UNDP emphasizes localized approaches, engaging local institutions and communities in conflict resolution. Activities focus on sustainable peace through 'little p' actions, which include peacebuilding, conflict prevention, and enhancing community resilience.

However, efforts must confront gender inequality and address the role of women in conflict resolution amidst restrictive social norms. Successful cases cited involve various countries, demonstrating the potential of the HDP nexus in fostering peace and stability in crisis conditions.

Title: Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus Approaches in Conflict and Disaster Settings [ES]
Abstract:
The evaluation explores the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus approach in crisis and disaster-affected contexts. Initiated by the UN in 2016, this approach aims to improve coordination and integration among humanitarian aid, development, and peacebuilding efforts. The UNDP plays a pivotal role in the nexus by fostering partnerships with local authorities, NGOs, and the private sector, aiming to create integrated solutions to long-standing conflicts and developmental challenges.

The document highlights the importance of adapting frameworks for coordination and moving beyond compartmentalized funding. It also emphasizes the significance of empowering local institutions and leveraging traditional governance structures to enhance societal cohesion.

The evaluation underlines the necessity of including women in conflict resolution and addressing gender inequalities. Successful examples include initiatives in countries like Nigeria, Lebanon, and Yemen, which utilized multi-sectoral responses, zone-based planning, and strengthened local capacities to tackle complex crises and improve resilience.

Title: Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus Approaches in Conflict and Disaster Settings [FR]
Abstract:
This evaluation explores the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus approach as implemented by the UNDP in conflict and disaster settings. It aims to reduce humanitarian needs by addressing the root causes and vulnerabilities faced by affected populations. 

The HDP nexus improves coordination among humanitarian, development, and peace actions, crucial in prolonged crises. The UNDP employs a multidimensional strategy, leveraging partnerships with local actors, civil society, and the private sector, particularly enhancing community resilience in regions like Nigeria, Yemen, and South Sudan. 

The approach includes adapting coordination frameworks, overcoming funding segmentation, engaging traditional and local institutions, and promoting durable peace through both 'Big P' and 'Little p' interventions. It underscores the importance of women\'s roles in conflict resolution and gender equality, and stresses the need for flexible, long-term financing. Collaborative efforts are shown in multiple countries like Turkey, Egypt, and Lebanon, demonstrating the broad application and challenges of the HDP nexus.

Title: Humanitarian–Development Nexus Approach to Health Systems Strengthening in Sudan: A Policy Analysis
Abstract:
This peer-reviewed article (Frontiers in Public Health, published May 2025 online; originally conducted in 2022) presents a policy analysis of how the HD nexus approach was adopted for health systems strengthening in Sudan — a context of protracted emergencies, volatile political transitions, and complex economic dynamics. Based on seven qualitative interviews with humanitarian and development health actors in 2022, it finds widespread conceptual ambiguity around the nexus despite consensus on its importance. National ownership and partner coordination are identified as key enablers, while a lack of guidance and inconsistent implementation remain barriers.

The article calls for more specific country-level guidance, dialogue, and flexibility in implementing the nexus approach in highly volatile contexts. Complements the Sudan health-nexus case already in the DB with a rigorous peer-reviewed analysis.

Title: IASC Country Brief on the HDP Nexus 2024: Burkina Faso
Abstract:
This 2024 IASC Country Brief examines the HDP nexus in Burkina Faso, one of the world's fastest-growing humanitarian crises, with 6.3 million people (one in four) in need of humanitarian assistance and over 2 million internally displaced.

The country faces an expanding security crisis with increasing civilian casualties, farmer-herder tensions, intercommunal conflict, and climate-induced vulnerabilities. The UN has developed the United Nations Interim Action Plan for Sustainable Development (UNIDAP 2023–2025) as a framework for recovery, stabilisation, and development, built on four pillars of peace, people, planet, and prosperity.

The brief documents the nexus approach under the political constraints of the transitional government, including the challenges of maintaining humanitarian access and development partnerships in an increasingly restrictive operating environment.

Title: IASC Country Brief on the HDP Nexus 2024: Burundi
Abstract: This 2024 IASC Country Brief examines HDP nexus operationalisation in Burundi, where a HDP Nexus Steering Committee was established in 2021 to develop a common approach and define strategic collective outcomes. The brief documents how government leadership, while important for legitimacy, ultimately delayed nexus implementation — as coordination could only be operationalised with certain actors under conditions acceptable to the government. It captures the fundamental tension between government-led nexus approaches (which support state legitimacy and ownership) and the humanitarian imperative to reach populations regardless of political sensitivities. The Burundi case offers lessons for nexus practitioners on balancing government ownership with principled humanitarian action.

The brief documents the nexus framework built around the Recovery and Peacebuilding Assessment (RPBA) and its links to collective outcomes, the DDR programme, and efforts to restore state authority. It analyses the challenges of pursuing development-oriented approaches while the security situation remains volatile, and examines how the nexus has been used to identify durable solutions platforms for displacement.

Title: IASC Country Brief on the HDP Nexus 2024: Chad
Abstract:
This 2024 IASC Country Brief documents the HDP nexus approach in Chad, one of the countries with the most comprehensive and long-standing nexus frameworks in Africa, dating to 2016. Chad faces a complex and protracted humanitarian situation with inadequate social infrastructure, climate shocks, and conflict spillover from neighbouring countries. While a national HDP nexus roadmap was drawn up in 2019, a national nexus strategy remains to be finalised.

The brief notes subnational variations, with the Lake Chad province cited as a reference model for nexus coordination to be replicated in other provinces. It documents progress made in securing shared visions among humanitarian, development, and peace actors, and provides recommendations for accelerating nexus implementation at country and subnational levels.

Abstract:
This 2024 IASC Country Brief examines the HDP nexus approach in the DRC, one of the world's most complex humanitarian crises marked by armed conflict, displacement, governance challenges, and climate vulnerability. It documents the HDP nexus governance architecture in DRC, including the multi-stakeholder HDP Nexus core team co-chaired by the Resident Coordinator and EU.

Title: IASC Country Brief on the HDP Nexus 2024: El Salvador
Abstract:
This 2024 IASC Country Brief examines the HDP nexus in El Salvador, a context undergoing significant change following major reductions in homicidal violence under President Bukele's security strategy. While multidimensional poverty has decreased, monetary poverty remains a challenge, gender-based violence persists, and the country remains highly vulnerable to climate risks threatening food security and livelihoods. 

The brief documents how the nexus approach has been adapted to this transitional context — moving from a primarily protection-focused response to one increasingly oriented towards recovery, resilience, and long-term development — while maintaining attention to the residual protection needs of women and girls. It offers lessons for nexus practitioners working in contexts transitioning from acute conflict to complex post-violence recovery.

Abstract:
This 2024 IASC Country Brief examines HDP nexus approaches in Haiti, one of the world's most acute humanitarian crises — shaped by President Moïse's 2021 assassination, rampant gang violence (300+ gangs), cholera resurgence, and extreme food insecurity affecting half the population.

The brief documents how nexus approaches have attempted to function amid an acute protection crisis and contested state legitimacy, covering collective outcome frameworks, gang-sensitive programming, coordination between humanitarian and development actors, and the particular challenges of maintaining nexus coherence when the primary drivers of need are criminal violence rather than armed conflict. Haiti is a case study in the limits of conventional nexus frameworks in settings with absent or criminally compromised state authority.

Title: IASC Country Brief on the HDP Nexus 2024: Iraq
Abstract:

Iraq no longer has a Humanitarian Response Plan for 2023; instead, a transitional document bridges humanitarian action and development programming.

The brief documents how the HDP nexus has been operationalised through the UNSDCF in partnership with the Government of Iraq, and analyses the challenges of ensuring that residual humanitarian needs (particularly for displaced populations and returnees) do not fall through the gap as the system transitions. Unlike most HDP nexus contexts, the peace pillar in Vanuatu relates primarily to gender-based violence and violence against children rather than armed conflict.

Published in 2021, it provides a pre-war baseline: the April 2023 outbreak of conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces fundamentally disrupted the coordination architecture documented here, making this brief an important reference point for understanding what had been built before the crisis.

Written by the Co-Chairs of the IASC Taskforces on AAP (TF2), localisation (TF5), and the HDP nexus (TF4), the paper argues that all three approaches are mutually reinforcing drivers towards a humanitarian system held to account by those it serves. It provides concrete recommendations on how their linkages can be operationalised as the sector prepares for a new Emergency Relief Coordinator.

Abstract:
This IASC Guidance Note (March 2024) provides direction to IASC global clusters on how to advance the HDP nexus approach within their coordination mandates. It explains how clusters — traditionally focused on sectoral humanitarian coordination — can embed nexus thinking into their strategic frameworks, coordination platforms, and programming guidance.

The note addresses practical entry points including joint analysis, collective outcomes, and engagement with development and peace actors at both global and country levels. It is an important system-wide guidance document designed to translate the IASC's nexus commitments into cluster-level operational practice across health, food security, shelter, WASH, protection, and other cluster areas.

Abstract:

It serves as an update to the 2021 mapping and assesses progress, outcomes achieved, remaining barriers, and enablers for scale-up.

Title: Implementation Roadmap For Nutrition Centric-Humanitarian, Development And Peace Triple Nexus Operationalization In Ethiopia
Abstract: The document presents an implementation roadmap for the Nutrition Centric-Humanitarian, Development, and Peace Triple Nexus (NC-HDPTN) approach in Ethiopia. It outlines strategies for collaborating humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding actors to enhance food security, nutrition, and resilience among vulnerable populations in the country. The roadmap details a multi-phase plan, including inception, implementation, and dissemination phases running from 2023 to 2030. It emphasizes the importance of joint situation assessment, need analysis, scalable multi-sector programming, flexible financing mechanisms, and conflict-sensitive approaches. The roadmap aims for specific outcomes like improved food and nutrition security, enhanced community resilience, and sustainable peacebuilding, with targeted reductions in child malnutrition rates and increased community participation in peace initiatives. The plan involves various stakeholders, including government bodies, NGOs, donors, and local communities, with a focus on sustainable and locally driven solutions. Key metrics and performance indicators are defined to track progress and impact throughout the initiative.

Title: Implementing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in a Post-Pandemic World: Multilateral Cooperation and the Challenge of Inter-organisational Dialogue
Abstract:
This paper examines the implementation of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus in a post-pandemic world, as called for by the UN Secretary General. Implemented since 2016, the HDP Nexus is an innovative policy framework aiming for multilateral cooperation across humanitarian, development, and peace sectors.

The paper discusses strengths and challenges in interorganisational dialogue among major institutions like the UN, EU, and World Bank, in pre- and post-COVID-19 contexts. It highlights the need for effective cooperation and local actor involvement to achieve peace and empowerment in conflict areas. Insights are drawn from activities in Myanmar, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Cameroon.

The paper urges these institutions to capitalize on comparative advantages for better Nexus deliveries and addresses the complexities involved in aligning policies among multilaterals. Ultimately, the paper explores the experimentalist governance approach, emphasizing iterative learning and participative policymaking as necessary for sustainable peace and development.

Title: Improving your Programmatic Learning Journey: A Resource Guide for HDP Nexus Practitioners
Abstract:
This practical guide from the Knowledge Platform Security and Rule of Law (KPSRL), commissioned by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is designed to help humanitarian, development and peacebuilding practitioners strengthen programmatic learning within HDP nexus contexts.

Based on in-depth research with seven organisations and a systematic literature review, the guide addresses a critical gap: despite widespread commitment to adaptive management and learning in the nexus field, few organisations have effective systems for capturing, sharing, and acting on programme learning.

The guide provides strategies, frameworks, and case studies on how programmatic learning happens in practice — covering how organisations conduct learning activities, what enables or prevents meaningful uptake of findings, and how learning translates into programme adaptation. It offers tailored recommendations for practitioners, policymakers, and the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs on creating institutional cultures and systems that support continuous improvement in nexus programming.
