Title: In the Eye of the Storm: Humanitarian NGOs, Complex Emergencies, and Conflict Resolution
Abstract:
This journal article by Janice Gross Stein explores the challenges and dilemmas faced by humanitarian NGOs in complex emergencies arising from internal violence and state failures. As major powers disengage, these NGOs play a crucial role in delivering relief, yet they face criticism for inadvertently exacerbating conflict through asset transfer and inadequate coordination. 

The paper discusses strategies that NGOs can adopt, such as adjusting the type of aid provided to minimize looting and collaborating with local authorities. It also emphasizes the need for greater security arrangements, potentially involving regional or private security forces, to ensure aid does not fuel conflict.

The author suggests that NGOs must balance their humanitarian ethics with the harsh realities of politically manipulating relief operations to avoid doing harm. Ultimately, Stein argues that while humanitarian efforts face many challenges, thoughtful choices in programming and collaboration can mitigate negative externalities and enhance conflict resolution.

Abstract:
The guide on INFF Assessment and diagnostics provides a framework for analyzing a country's financing landscape. It discusses the scope, value, and practical implementation of financing landscape assessments, highlighting their role in identifying financing gaps and opportunities for effective alignment with sustainable development goals (SDGs). 

The guide details various financing sources, including public and private funds, and emphasizes the significance of remittances, blended finance, and impact investments. Challenges in data availability and comparability are considered, alongside methodological tools for comprehensive assessments.

The document stresses the importance of stakeholder engagement and differentiated analyses tailored to specific country contexts, including fragile and conflict-affected areas. Lessons learned from prior assessments underscore the need for inclusive and accessible financial analyses that inform strategic, integrated approaches to national sustainable development financing.

Title: Inform Report 2024
Abstract:
The INFORM Report 2024 marks the tenth anniversary of the INFORM Risk Index, an initiative to quantify humanitarian crisis risks globally. The index facilitates informed decision-making by aggregating data on crisis severity from various credible sources. Over the decade, the index has evolved into a pivotal tool for strategic planning, combining scientific analyses to improve crisis management outcomes.

The European Union continues to play a substantial role in humanitarian aid, stressing development investments to tackle root causes of crises. Recent updates reflect the growing impact of climatic changes and socio-economic challenges on crises, highlighting the increased risk severity globally. Conflict remains a predominant driver behind the escalating humanitarian crisis risks, while advances in infrastructure and institutions provide some resilience.

This comprehensive report underscores the necessity for evidence-based strategies to build a sustainable future amidst complex global challenges.

Title: Integrating Conflict Prevention and Peacebuilding into United Nations Development Assistance
Abstract:
This document examines how conflict prevention and peacebuilding can be systematically integrated into UN development assistance at the country level. It addresses the institutional, operational and programmatic challenges of ensuring that UN development actors — working through the UNDAF/UNSDCF — contribute actively to conflict prevention and peacebuilding, beyond merely avoiding harm.

Key themes include: the role of the UN Resident Coordinator system in promoting coherent peace-development linkages; joint conflict analysis; collective outcomes that include peacebuilding dimensions; and the challenge of balancing development mandates with conflict prevention objectives. The document provides guidance for UN country teams on operationalising the peace pillar of the HDP Nexus.

It also elaborates on monitoring and evaluating integration, promoting equity, and addresses challenges and dilemmas in peacebuilding integration, such as balancing comprehensive peace plans with sector-specific mandates.

The guide further discusses the institutional shifts required to mainstream conflict sensitivity and how integrated programming can enhance program coherence and effectiveness.

Title: Integrating the P of the HDP Nexus in Ukraine: WeWorld Experiences and Reflections Integrating Social Cohesion and Peace-Oriented Activities within its Programme in Ukraine
Abstract:
Practice-oriented report (WeWorld, 2026) providing practical guidance on integrating the peace dimension of the HDP nexus in Ukraine. Grounded in a peer-learning and consultation roundtable convened by WeWorld in December 2025 — bringing together Ukrainian peacebuilding and dialogue practitioners alongside international humanitarian, development and peacebuilding actors — and in WeWorld's own programme experience since March 2022.

The report argues that integrating the "P" is less about adding a new thematic strand and more about changing how humanitarian and early recovery work is planned, delivered and adapted. In the Ukrainian context, where it can be politically sensitive to speak explicitly about "conflict" and "peace," the report frames peace integration primarily as "small p" practice centred on social cohesion and trust.

Entry points covered include: mainstreaming conflict sensitivity across the programme cycle; treating MHPSS as a cohesion enabler; building partnerships with local Ukrainian peacebuilding practitioners; localisation and subgranting to strengthen community-led initiatives; accountability to affected populations; staff care and burnout prevention; light-touch community dialogue and dispute management; and peace education with children. Directed at donors and peer organisations, and closes with an action agenda for more coherent, locally grounded, peace-responsive practice across Ukraine's aid response.

Title: Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women and Girls
Abstract:
The document serves as a companion piece to the 2020 Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women and Girls (GEEWG). It emphasizes the need to mainstream GEEWG within the triple nexus framework combining humanitarian, development, and peace efforts. Despite broad consensus on its importance, significant barriers such as lack of strategic discussion, coordination, resources, and understanding of GEEWG integration hinder progress.

The document proposes the establishment of a Task Force to lead country-level pilots, aiming to clarify and operationalize gender mainstreaming within the nexus. Insights from these pilots could foster transformative change and enhance gender accountability mechanisms. The suggested actions target key bodies such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee and UN agencies to encourage further understanding and implementation of GEEWG initiatives. These efforts are crucial to scale-up gender equality mainstreaming, ensuring that it becomes a cross-cutting theme in nexus processes globally, with improved strategic vision and resource allocation.

Title: Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) Country Brief on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus: Colombia
Abstract:
The IASC Country Brief on Colombia addresses the complex interplay of armed conflict, migration, illegal business, and natural disasters affecting human rights and civilian protection. The Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus approach aims to align strategic priorities of peace, migration, and sustainable development through the UNSDCF, HRP, and RMRP plans.

Key steps in operationalizing the nexus include leadership coordination, joint analysis, collective outcomes focusing on PDETs affected by conflict and violence, and integrated planning and programming at national and regional levels. Lessons highlight the importance of local coordination networks, national NGO involvement, and alignment with government plans, while challenges remain in shared understanding of nexus implementation.

Gender considerations are embedded across plans, ensuring mainstreaming and tailored outcomes. The brief emphasizes local actors' involvement to enhance project sustainability, accountability, and resilience.

Title: Interlinking Humanitarian Aid, Development Cooperation, and Peacebuilding in Displacement Contexts: The Added Value of the HDP Nexus' Peace Component
Abstract:
The commentary explores the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus with a focus on forced displacement contexts. With forced displacement reaching record numbers, there is a need for enhanced coordination across humanitarian aid, development cooperation, and peacebuilding. The HDP nexus introduces a peace component, aiming to address structural causes of displacement and ensure durable solutions, such as local integration, return, or resettlement. Both 'small p' and 'big P' peace measures are discussed, with 'small p' emphasizing social cohesion and local conflict management, and 'big P' focusing on broader national/regional peacebuilding.

The German government is encouraged to support the UN's Action Agenda on Internal Displacement, decentralize decision-making, use 'trilingual' experts, and overcome organizational disincentives. The HDP nexus offers a comprehensive approach for addressing displacement, enhancing collaboration, and fulfilling the needs for peace and security as preconditions for refugee return.

Title: International Assistance in Gaza: Aiding Fragmentation or Unity?
Abstract:
This paper examines how international assistance in Gaza has interacted with the political fragmentation of Palestinian governance and the ongoing conflict context. It analyses whether and how aid has contributed to or mitigated the political division between the West Bank and Gaza, and the implications for humanitarian principles, development programming and peacebuilding in the Palestinian context. 

Key issues include: the political economy of aid in a deeply fragmented governance context; humanitarian-development linkages in an environment of protracted siege and active conflict; donor coordination challenges; and the tension between impartial humanitarian response and the political dimensions of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The paper draws lessons for conflict-sensitive programming in politically complex environments.

Title: International Network on Conflict and Fragility (INCAF) Ensuring Fragile states are not left behind
Abstract:
The report by the OECD International Network on Conflict and Fragility (INCAF) outlines the dynamics of financial resource flows in fragile states. It analyzes the impact of various crises, such as global financial, food, and fuel crises, on aid, trade, foreign direct investment, and domestic revenues in fragile countries.

The report highlights that many fragile states face significant challenges in meeting the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) due to structural issues, with growth rates and domestic revenue generation being insufficient. ODA (Official Development Assistance) remains concentrated in a few countries, and there is variability in aid effectiveness due to donors' fragmented focus and aid volatility in these regions.

The report suggests that aid could play a catalytic role by fostering domestic revenue mobilization and encouraging trade and investment in fragile states, ultimately reducing aid dependency and supporting post-conflict transitions. It also discusses the evolving engagement of non-DAC donors, notably China's increasing role in fragile states, while emphasizing the need for coherent international policies to maximize developmental impacts and mitigate negative effects.

Title: IOM Ukraine and Neighbouring Countries Crisis Response Plan 2026
Abstract:
This IOM Crisis Response Plan for Ukraine and Neighbouring Countries 2026 sets out IOM's humanitarian, recovery and nexus programming priorities and targets for the year, covering Ukraine and the countries hosting Ukrainian displaced populations including Moldova, Poland, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, and other neighbouring states.

It outlines IOM's programming across its key mandated areas including emergency shelter and non-food items, health and psychosocial support, protection, livelihoods, and displacement tracking, with specific attention to the challenges of maintaining nexus approaches in an active conflict environment where humanitarian principles must remain paramount.

Title: IRC 2025 Emergency Watchlist
Abstract:
The International Rescue Committee's annual Emergency Watchlist identifies the 20 countries most at risk of new or worsening humanitarian emergencies, using a rigorous methodology combining 74 quantitative and qualitative variables. The 2025 edition documents how humanitarian needs are increasingly concentrated in Emergency Watchlist countries — at the intersection of fragility, conflict, climate vulnerability, and declining ODA — and outlines key imbalances the sector must address. 

For nexus practitioners, the Watchlist's policy recommendations are directly relevant: they call for development actors to commit half of all bilateral ODA to fragile and conflict-affected states; for donors to fund anticipatory action for climate-vulnerable communities; and for localisation reforms that genuinely shift decision-making power. Title: Joining Forces to Combat Protracted Crises: Humanitarian and Development Support for Water and Sanitation Providers in the Middle East and North Africa
Abstract:
This report, published by the World Bank in collaboration with organizations like UNICEF, focuses on addressing prolonged crises affecting water and sanitation services in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). It identifies five critical challenges: inadequate water resource management, aggressive competition from alternative providers, failures of high-tech sewage treatment plants, rising energy costs during independent electricity generation, and dwindling cash flows.

The study recommends forming stronger partnerships between humanitarian and development entities to build resilience before crises occur and to sustain services during them. With rapid urbanization over the last two decades, many service providers have become vulnerable to prolonged crises due to reliance on subsidies and lack of accountability, leading to inefficiencies. The report underscores the need for these service providers to coordinate with international actors to circumvent potential collapses and emphasizes planning and preparedness for future shocks.

Title: Joint Recovery and Peacebuilding Assessments: a practical note to assessment and planning
Abstract:
The Joint Recovery and Peacebuilding Assessments (RPBA) offer a structured approach for evaluating and addressing recovery and peacebuilding needs in conflict-affected countries. This practical note, developed by the United Nations, World Bank, and European Union, advocates a coordinated international response, emphasizing early engagement, stakeholder inclusion, and the development of national institutions to ensure sustainable peacebuilding.

The RPBA serves as a flexible framework for prioritizing needs, planning recovery strategies, and facilitating international support, aiming to ensure inclusivity and effective governance throughout the process. It consists of three phases: pre-evaluation, evaluation prioritization and planning, and validation and completion, which collectively help inform and drive recovery efforts through a unified strategic approach.

The document also highlights the importance of conflict sensitivity and gender analysis, and suggests methodologies for conflict assessment to ensure interventions do not exacerbate existing tensions. Broad stakeholder engagement, including women and youth, is encouraged to enhance ownership and sustainability of the peacebuilding process.

Title: JSC Review: Refined Recommendations for 7 Countries
Abstract:
The document presents recommendations for seven countries on enhancing regional coordination, accountability, and financing through the United Nations frameworks and partnerships. In Burkina Faso, a coordinated approach involving the RCs of Burkina Faso, Niger, and Mali is emphasized for addressing cross-border issues. Strengthened humanitarian-development-peace nexus financing is suggested as a pilot case.

Recommendations for Cameroon include developing joint vulnerability analysis across the Lake Chad Region. Chad is advised to create a Joint Analysis Team for collective outcome adjustments and host a high-level donor meeting. Ethiopia should align initiatives into an Integrated Package and connect regional initiatives to strengthen partnerships. In Niger, strengthening local government capacity and aligning to the African Union's strategy is key. Recommendations for Nigeria focus on expanding resilience capacities and establishing pooled funds for integrated responses. Somalia faces famine-like conditions, necessitating advocacy with the World Bank for immediate and long-term food insecurity solutions and support for its National Development Plan to gain concessional financing access.

Title: JSC reviews: synthesis of findings and recommendations
Abstract:
The synthesis of findings and recommendations of the JSC reviews in seven countries aims to bring together humanitarian, development, and peace actors under collective outcomes. These outcomes are intended to reduce vulnerabilities and accelerate progress towards the SDGs.

The report highlights the need for a transformative approach focusing on prevention, peacebuilding, human rights, and gender considerations that were not prominently addressed. It stresses the importance of integrating regional and global processes, such as the UN Integrated Strategy for the Sahel and the Famine Action Mechanism, into country-level responses. 

Key recommendations revolve around leadership, strengthening government and Resident Coordinator Office capacities, enhancing joint information and analysis through risk-informed and gender-sensitive approaches, articulating and operationalizing collective outcomes, harmonizing resources and financing, and establishing accountability frameworks.

These recommendations seek to foster integrated actions, strengthen collaboration, adjust programming and resource flows to align with collective outcomes, and ensure evidence-based monitoring towards minimizing humanitarian crises and promoting durable solutions.

Title: Key Questions and Considerations for Donors at the Triple Nexus: Lessons from UK and Sweden
Abstract:
This Development Initiatives synthesis report draws on detailed case studies of the UK and Sweden to distil key questions, observations and practical considerations for all donors seeking to operationalise the Triple Nexus. It examines donor approaches across three areas: policy frameworks; programme and allocation cycles; and organisational structures and systems.

Key findings include that the nexus is better understood in practice than in concept, with bottom-up collaborative solutions outpacing headquarters-level policy development; that peace remains the least developed pillar; and that funding mechanisms are not yet aligned with nexus ambitions. The paper provides a set of cross-cutting lessons for donors at strategic, principled, and practical levels.

Title: La Agenda de Mujeres, Paz y Seguridad en la Implementación del Triple Nexo HDP en la Cooperación Española (CEIPAZ)
Abstract:
This CEIPAZ research project and resource hub (2025–2026) examines the intersection of the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda with the HDP triple nexus in Spanish development cooperation.

Funded by AECID's 2024 innovation call, the project generates applied knowledge for Spanish cooperation actors on the practical integration of the WPS agenda and the triple nexus, with a focus on gender dynamics in humanitarian crises, development, and peacebuilding. Outputs include: a literature review on WPS; analytical notes on the triple nexus, MPS and humanitarian action, and the Mozambique experience; a policy brief on the triple nexus with gender; and a practical guide for Spanish cooperation actors.

The project hub page links to all published outputs and provides a Spanish-language reference point for WPS-nexus integration.

Title: La aplicación del “triple nexo” en la Cooperación Española
Abstract:
Este estudio analiza la aceptación y el conocimiento del enfoque de triple nexo entre la acción humanitaria, el desarrollo y la paz por los actores de la cooperación española y explora los retos que identifican para operativizar este planteamiento especialmente en términos de financiación, planificación y coordinación. En términos generales, el informe plantea las fortalezas y debilidades para avanzar en la aplicación del enfoque nexo en la CE, en línea con los elementos establecidos por la Recomendación del CAD-OCDE sobre el tema.

Las recomendaciones incluyen replantear algunas de las herramientas de planificación, coordinación y financiación de la cooperación española para que sean más adecuadas a la implementación del enfoque de triple nexo.  Asimismo, para la efectiva operativización es fundamental continuar impulsando el trabajo de colaboración con el CAD, difundir más ampliamente el conocimiento y el debate sobre el triple nexo HDP entre los actores de la cooperación, así como dedicar recursos financieros y humanos específicos. En concreto, el componente de paz requiere de un mayor desarrollo, lo que ofrece una oportunidad para fortalecer la construcción de la paz como aspecto central de la cooperación española.

El estudio ha sido realizado con el apoyo y la colaboración de la Oficina de Acción Humanitaria (OAH) de la AECID.

Title: Lake Chad Programme strategy 2018-2023
Abstract:
The "Lake Chad Programme Strategy 2018-2023" by Plan International lays out a comprehensive approach to tackle the severe humanitarian crisis in the Lake Chad Basin, encompassing regions in Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, and Chad. The strategy aims to improve the lives of vulnerable populations, specifically focusing on children and adolescent girls, by addressing issues such as gender equality, education, protection from violence and economic empowerment. 

Four strategic programme objectives guide the initiative: equal access to education, improvement of child protection, promotion of economic rehabilitation, and empowerment through participation and leadership. The approach integrates humanitarian and development efforts while fostering social cohesion and resilience, advocating for public policies and partnerships, and focusing on gender-transformative programming.

Through collaboration with governments and stakeholders, Plan International seeks to mitigate risks and allocate financial resources effectively over five years to achieve these goals.

Title: Le Nexus Humanitaire-Développement-Paix: Quelles implications pour les organisations multi-mandatées?
Abstract:
The document discusses the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, emphasizing the need for simultaneous humanitarian aid, development programs, and peace-building efforts to address the vulnerabilities and conflicts intensifying due to climatic shocks and socio-political unrest.

The nexus aims to integrate immediate assistance with long-term investments to tackle systemic causes of vulnerability and promote sustainable peace. Structural changes are proposed for aid systems, impacting how aid is coordinated and financed. Key players like the United Nations and the World Bank are adopting new structures and financing methods to enhance the effectiveness of combined humanitarian and development efforts.

The document explores the implications of this approach for multi-mandated organizations like Oxfam, highlighting the necessity for holistic contextual analysis, adaptive management, and collaborative partnerships. Challenges include maintaining principled humanitarian actions amidst political pressures and ensuring equitable consideration of gender issues and conflict dynamics in planning and execution.

The nexus promises more effective aid by addressing immediate and systemic needs, but requires careful balance in its operationalization to avoid compromising humanitarian principles and reaching vulnerable populations effectively.

Title: Le Triple Nexus au Mali : Coordination, Sécuritisation et Lignes Floues (French)
Abstract: Version française du rapport du Centre for Humanitarian Action (CHA) sur le Triple Nexus au Mali. Le rapport examine comment les approches nexus se déroulent dans un contexte marqué par de multiples conflits armés, des opérations militaires et des risques de sécuritisation de l'aide humanitaire et au développement. Il analyse les défis de coordination entre acteurs HDP, les risques liés au brouillage des lignes civilo-militaires, et les tensions entre principes humanitaires et approches nexus dans un contexte d'insécurité chronique au Sahel.

Title: Leaving no crisis behind with assistance for the triple nexus: Humanitarian, development and peace funding in crisis contexts
Abstract:
The report emphasizes the growing humanitarian needs due to crises such as climate-related disasters, conflicts, and food insecurity, and points out the inadequacy of humanitarian funding alone to address these needs. While donors have significantly increased official development assistance (ODA), the share directed to protracted crisis countries is the lowest in five years, with a marked shift towards more humanitarian assistance rather than development and peace support. Many countries facing crises are not receiving sufficient development assistance, leaving them behind in addressing extreme poverty.

The report calls for a balanced approach to financing under the humanitarian-development-peace nexus to tackle root causes of crises, build resilience, and prioritize prevention not only through humanitarian aid but aligning efforts with development and peace agendas.

The report suggests strengthening country-specific nexus financing strategies, improving finance tracking and coordination, and reconsidering the balance between grants and loans to foster more sustainable support for vulnerable countries. Additionally, it highlights the need for more adequate funding for climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction, which remains misaligned with the vulnerability levels of crisis countries.

Title: Lecciones extraídas de evaluaciones: Adaptación de los ODS a los contextos Locales a través de la gobernanza local [ES]
Abstract:
The document outlines five lessons from initiatives that support the localization of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through local governance. It emphasizes the need for coordination across different governance levels, the involvement of local stakeholders, the importance of building government capacity, the use of data for planning, and leveraging voluntary local reviews.

Successful localization of SDGs requires vertical integration of policies and alignment between international, national, and local frameworks. The UNDP's efforts in multiple countries highlight the benefits of engaging diverse actors and sectors, fostering community ownership, and ensuring adaptive and transparent local governance.

Challenges such as fragmented support or lack of structured participation may hinder progress, but structured initiatives can enhance transparency, accountability, and intergovernmental cooperation, advancing local adaptation and sustainable development.

Title: Left to Bridge the Gap - Humanitarian Assistance in Politically Estranged Settings
Abstract:
This NYU Center on International Cooperation (CIC) paper examines the specific challenge of delivering humanitarian assistance in 'politically estranged' settings — contexts where the host government has lost international legitimacy or has been subject to sanctions, diplomatic isolation, or political disengagement by key donors. Such settings — including Afghanistan under Taliban rule, Myanmar under the military junta, and Sudan under the current conflict — represent an acute challenge for nexus approaches, since the development and peace pillars of the nexus typically require engagement with state authorities that may be impossible or inappropriate.

The paper analyses how humanitarian organisations are 'left to bridge the gap' in these contexts, often being asked to deliver far beyond their traditional life-saving mandate while development and political engagement have withdrawn. It examines the risks and limitations of this humanitarian over-stretch, the implications for principled action, and the options available to the international community for maintaining meaningful engagement while managing the political constraints of estranged relationships.

Title: Lessons and Recommendations for Implementing Kenya's New Refugee Law
Abstract:
This Refugees International field report (August 2024), based on interviews in March 2024 in Nairobi, Kakuma, and Dadaab, assesses progress and challenges in implementing Kenya's Refugee Act 2021 (regulations published 2024) and the two integrated settlement programmes — the Kalobeyei Integrated Socio-Economic Development Programme (KISEDEP) and the Garissa Integrated Socio-Economic Development Plan (GISEDEP). These programmes are Kenya's primary vehicles for operationalising the humanitarian-development nexus for refugees and host communities, shifting from camp-based assistance toward self-reliance and settlement.

The report provides field-level evidence on social cohesion gains (market sharing, reduced inter-community conflict), structural barriers (limited access to employment rights despite legal reform), and the governance challenges of implementation. Kenya's is one of the few case studies of a government-led HD nexus legal framework.

Title: Lessons from Evaluations: SDG Localization through Local Governance
Abstract:
The paper provides lessons from United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) initiatives that support the localization of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through local governance.

It highlights five key lessons: firstly, the necessity of policy coordination and alignment across governance levels for effective SDG implementation. Secondly, engaging diverse stakeholders increases local ownership and enhances SDG integration. Thirdly, local government capacity building is crucial for transparency and citizen trust. Fourthly, generating and utilizing SDG data boosts capacity and coherence in planning and monitoring. Lastly, Voluntary Local Reviews (VLRs) are seen as a promising tool for accelerating SDG localization progress, facilitating transparency and enhancing integration from local to national levels.

The paper synthesizes insights and evaluates from different countries and contexts, offering perspectives on the challenges and successes of SDG localization through local governance.

Title: Lessons from the COVID-19 Crisis: 6 Opportunities to Strengthen Conflict Sensitivity across the HDP Nexus
Abstract:
This policy brief by NYU's Center on International Cooperation (CIC) argues that the COVID-19 pandemic, and the associated lockdowns, border closures, and socioeconomic shocks, increased risks of violent conflict globally and made it crucial for the UN to adopt a conflict-sensitive lens across the entire HDP Nexus. 

Drawing on engagement with UN actors throughout 2021, the brief identifies six specific opportunities through which the crisis can strengthen conflict sensitivity: strengthening joint analysis, improving collective outcomes, leveraging prevention, enhancing local engagement, improving funding flexibility, and strengthening accountability. The paper positions COVID-19 as a potential turning point for deeper cross-pillar integration in UN programming.

Title: Lessons Learned and recommendations from The Humanitarian-Development Nexus For Nutrition
Abstract:
The report analyzes the opportunities and challenges in strengthening the Humanitarian-Development Nexus (HDN) within the nutrition sector through case studies in Afghanistan, Myanmar, and Niger. It reveals the need for integrating short-term humanitarian responses with long-term development strategies to achieve sustainable nutrition outcomes.

The study identifies gaps in multisectoral policies and highlights the necessity for collaborative, inclusive spaces that involve various actors. Recommendations include developing a shared understanding of HDN, building collaboration around common objectives, and ensuring accountability and inclusion. The report underscores the importance of risk-informed approaches and proactive participation by governments and stakeholders in aligning nutrition-related national policies with disaster preparedness.

Title: LGBTQI+ People and the Triple Nexus of Development Cooperation, Humanitarian Action and Peacebuilding
Abstract:
This peer-reviewed article in the Journal of Humanitarian Affairs (2025) examines the largely absent perspective of LGBTQI+ people and sexual and gender minorities within triple nexus approaches to development cooperation, humanitarian action, and peacebuilding. Drawing on existing literature — primarily from Colombia — the authors analyse four arguments for inclusion: LGBTQI+ people are targets of violence in conflict; their inclusion is ethically required; some were combatants; and they have valuable, often untapped capacities for building inclusive post-conflict societies.

The article argues that all three pillars of the nexus fail to systematically include LGBTQI+ perspectives and makes recommendations for more inclusive programme design, needs assessment, and peacebuilding process design. It opens a new area of inquiry for nexus practitioners working on gender, protection, and social cohesion.

Title: Light Guidance on Advancing the HDPN Approach through the Food Security Cluster | Food Security Cluster
Abstract:
The document is a guide for Food Security Clusters (FSCs) concerning the operationalization of the Humanitarian, Development, and Peace Nexus (HDPN) approach from 2023 to 2025. It outlines strategies for enhancing coordination between HDP actors to address chronic food insecurity issues. Key objectives include improving collective understanding of food insecurity drivers, fostering joint monitoring, evaluation, and learning, and advocating for multi-year financing strategies.

The guide highlights the importance of comprehensive data analysis and collaboration with research institutions to understand the underlying causes of food crises and to develop targeted interventions. It emphasizes the need for strategic partnerships and capacity building within country FSCs to effectively implement HDPN activities while maintaining the humanitarian mandate.

The guide also suggests mapping platforms, actors, and potential donors to bolster financial support and alignment among humanitarian, development, and peace initiatives.

Title: Linking Social Protection and Humanitarian Assistance in the Philippines
Abstract: Report examining how the Philippines has progressively linked its national social protection system — particularly the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Programme (4Ps) conditional cash transfer — with humanitarian response mechanisms following major disasters and conflict situations. Provides a case study of a middle-income country operationalising the humanitarian-development nexus through social protection, combining a well-established government-led system with shock-responsive mechanisms for disaster and conflict response. Draws lessons on government leadership, system interoperability between humanitarian and development financing, and the conditions under which social protection can serve as a bridge between immediate relief and longer-term development.

Title: Linking Thinking: Why is it so hard and what can we do about it
Abstract:
This policy paper by Joanna Macrae addresses the challenges and potential solutions for integrating humanitarian, development, and peace efforts, referred to as 'linking thinking'. The importance of this integration arises from the changing landscape of global poverty, increasingly concentrated in fragile states, and exacerbated by prolonged crises and climate change.

The paper critiques previous 'linking thinking' strategies and highlights four major challenges: the problematic interaction of aid with fragile states, the unresolved humanitarian principles amid developmental goals, a need for reform in aid\'s administrative frameworks, and the feasibility of long-term developmental strategies in insecure environments. While recent international summits propose a collaborative approach centered on collective outcomes, the efficacy of these initiatives remains uncertain due to entrenched structural and theoretical barriers.

The paper stresses the need for empirical analysis in adapting aid to specific crisis contexts and suggests that progress hinges on closer dialogue between stakeholders and significant structural reforms in the aid architecture.

Title: Livelihoods for Peace
Abstract:
The 'Livelihoods for Peace' paper by Interpeace explores the integration of livelihood initiatives with peacebuilding efforts to improve stability in conflict-affected regions. It argues that fair access to livelihood opportunities is crucial for peace since they provide tangible benefits, helping reduce grievances, improve cooperation, and build self-confidence.

However, it highlights that livelihoods alone are insufficient for sustainable peace without addressing other dimensions like social cohesion, security, justice, and wellbeing. The paper proposes a theory of change where livelihood interventions-such as enhancing opportunities, strengthening regulation, promoting cooperative activities, and improving social protection-are combined with peacebuilding methods like mediation and dialogue. These combined efforts help consolidate peace by reducing conflicts, fostering trust, and enhancing social cohesion.

The document identifies strategic opportunities to leverage this approach globally, particularly in post-conflict recovery stages, while acknowledging challenges such as integration difficulties and sustainability concerns.

Title: Localisation – An Unfinished Agenda Beyond 2026
Abstract:
This IASC paper reviews progress on the localisation agenda — the commitment to increase the share of resources, decision-making, and leadership going to local and national humanitarian actors — and makes the case for what must change beyond 2026 to realise genuine transformation.

Despite years of Grand Bargain commitments, multiple evaluations have documented that localisation has remained largely superficial: funding flows to local actors have not significantly increased, local organisations remain excluded from key decision-making forums, and international actors continue to dominate coordination and programming in most humanitarian contexts. 

The paper reviews the evidence on where localisation has and has not progressed, identifies the structural barriers within the international humanitarian system that have prevented more fundamental change, and proposes a more ambitious and transformative agenda for advancing localisation beyond 2026 — including changes to funding modalities, risk management, accountability frameworks, and the power dynamics embedded in coordination structures. It has direct implications for how the HDP nexus is implemented, given the nexus framework's emphasis on supporting national and local capacities.

Title: Localisation Across the Humanitarian- Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:
The journal article explores the concept of localisation across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus, spotlighting its importance in responding to conflicts, particularly in the Arab region. It traces the historical discourse surrounding localisation within humanitarian aid, development, and peace efforts, emphasizing the need for integrative approaches to resolve conflicts. Challenges such as defining and valuing local capacities and maintaining political will are central to effective localisation. 

The article critiques top-down, Northern-driven aid systems, highlighting the capacity and role of local actors in crisis response. The Triple Nexus aims to harmonize humanitarian, developmental, and peace initiatives, but faces skepticism over securitisation and resource competition. The piece advocates a nuanced understanding of local realities, arguing that international donors must empower local actors without paternalism, using a pragmatic and transdisciplinary approach to build a sustainable conflict response ecosystem. It underscores local context knowledge, drawing lessons from conflicts in places like Iraq and Syria, and addresses the politics around global-local dynamics, calling for a rethink of localisation practice to improve multi-scalar conflict governance.

Title: Localisation and the HDP Nexus: Empowering Local Organisations to Support the HDP Nexus Approach
Abstract:
This research partnership between Columbia SIPA and the UNDP Nexus Academy, with collaboration from the Network for Empowered Aid Response, addresses a critical knowledge gap in humanitarian, development, and peace programming: how localized organizations understand, operationalize, and experience Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus approaches, and what support they need to lead Nexus programming at scale. The core research question asks: How can local-most aid organizations prepare to step up and replace international aid organizations in supporting vulnerable populations through HDP Nexus interventions? This question emerges from a moment of convergence of crises and opportunities, where overlapping and prolonged crises demand integrated responses, resource constraints force efficiency, and growing recognition that local actors possess comparative advantages international organizations cannot replicate: community trust, contextual knowledge, adaptive capacity, cost-effectiveness, and sustained presence before, during, and after disaster.

This report examines five countries purposefully selected to represent diverse combinations of civil society strength and government consolidation: Türkiye, Colombia, Afghanistan, Myanmar, and Syria. This typology enables comparative analysis of how different governance arrangements, civic space restrictions, and conflict dynamics affect local organizations’ capacity to implement Nexus approaches. Research (November 2025 to April 2026) employed mixed methods including desk research, literature review, stakeholder analysis, interviews with stakeholders across country contents, and data analysis of funding streams. Key stakeholders engaged included local and national civil society organizations (large national NGOs, refugee-led organizations, community-based groups), international organizations (UN agencies and INGOs), and academic/research institutions.

Title: Localising Aid: Is it worth the risk?
Abstract:
This paper explores the risks associated with localizing aid by transferring aid to local actors rather than international ones, challenging the perception that local aid is inherently riskier. It outlines a framework for donors to assess risks involved in aid localization using categories such as contextual, programmatic, institutional, and fiduciary risks.

By examining the case of Afghanistan, it demonstrates that local aid may offer lower programmatic, contextual, and institutional risks although carries slightly higher fiduciary risks, especially after applying mitigation measures. Strategies for risk management include better coordination with local political systems and understanding patronage networks to tackle corruption.

The paper emphasizes the importance of tailoring aid instruments to specific country contexts and fostering donor-recipient relations to ensure aid effectiveness, suggesting ways to balance strategic goals with risk management approaches.

Title: Localization Through Coordination? Implementing the Humanitarian‐Development‐Peace Nexus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
Abstract:
This academic study, based on research from Radboud University, examines the relationship between coordination structures and localisation within the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, asking whether and how the nexus's new coordination architectures create genuine space for local actor leadership.

The nexus has prompted significant investment in new or redesigned coordination mechanisms — HDP steering committees, collective outcome working groups, joint analysis platforms — with the explicit goal of bringing humanitarian, development and peace actors together. But these mechanisms have primarily served international actors, replicating existing power imbalances within a new institutional frame.

The study examines specific country contexts to assess whether nexus coordination has enabled or constrained local actor participation and leadership, drawing on fieldwork and stakeholder interviews to understand the lived experience of local actors navigating international nexus coordination. It contributes to both the academic literature on coordination and to the policy debate on how to design nexus coordination mechanisms that genuinely advance localisation rather than institutionalising international dominance in new forms.

Title: Localizing The Triple Nexus: A Policy Research on the Humanitarian, Development, and Peace Nexus in nine contexts
Abstract:
This comprehensive report delves into the Triple Nexus of humanitarian, development, and peace actions across nine different countries, illustrating how each nation uniquely navigates and implements these interconnected frameworks in the face of varied conflicts and social challenges.

Key studies highlight the geopolitical constraints affecting the delivery and impact of international aid, such as the European Union's strategies in Syria and the necessity for development actions in the Lake Chad region amidst the Boko Haram conflict. Bangladesh's situation underscores the complexities of refugee-host dynamics and the need for integrated peacebuilding approaches, while Cameroon exemplifies the limitations of militaristic responses to extremism. Mozambique's struggles with natural disasters and insurgencies reveal gaps in regional peace strategies, building an urgent case for the SADC to enhance its intervention mechanisms. 

Afghanistan's educational projects funded by the World Bank demonstrate strides towards sustainable development amid ongoing conflict, juxtaposed against Mali's grassroots gender-focused strategies that demand broader international financial support. Guatemala's fragile state is assessed through its insufficient adaptation to collective aid strategies, and the Philippines faces critical challenges in balancing development projects with indigenous rights and environmental sustainability.

Each case provides insights into the nuanced application of the Triple Nexus, urging a global dialogue on its principles to foster equitable and effective conflict resolution and development strategies.

Abstract:
This Norad-commissioned report examines the concept of the HDP Nexus through the lens of development cooperation, critically exploring what the nexus means for development actors and whether it represents a genuine paradigm shift or a rebranding of existing approaches.

Based on literature review, key informant interviews, and case analysis, the report traces the evolution of the nexus concept and its translation into development policy and programming. It provides a clear-eyed assessment of what the nexus requires from development actors, and offers recommendations for how development agencies can better position themselves in nexus environments without compromising their mandate or effectiveness.

Title: Making the Nexus Real: Moving from Theory to Practice
Abstract:
The report 'Making the Nexus Real: Moving from Theory to Practice' examines the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus concept as proposed by the UN and OECD. It analyzes the relationship and tensions between humanitarian aid, development assistance, and peacebuilding, emphasizing the need for these sectors to collaborate to address immediate needs while resolving root causes of crises.

The HDP Nexus seeks to create coherence, complementarity, and collaboration across sectors, leveraging their comparative advantages to reduce vulnerabilities and unmet needs. The report highlights programming best practices, the significance of coordination, and challenges such as the lack of conflict analysis skills, siloed funding streams, and the need for platforms facilitating joint planning and objectives.

Case studies from South Sudan and Ethiopia illustrate attempts to implement these concepts. Most notably, the addition of the peace pillar and the top-down approach of the HDP Nexus are discussed, aiming to foster unified strategies and by engaging multiple stakeholders effectively to achieve shared outcomes.

Title: Managing Expectations and Advancing Reform: A Criteria-Based Approach to the HDP Nexus
Abstract:
Chapter 8 of the Global Policy triple nexus e-book and a contribution from CHA founding director Ralf Südhoff, this piece argues that the HDP nexus must be grounded in realistic, criteria-based assessment of where and when it can actually be implemented. It develops a practical framework distinguishing macro-level nexus (national political and security processes) from meso-level (area-based coordination) and micro-level (project design), and argues that much confusion stems from actors attempting macro-level nexus in contexts where only micro-level is feasible.

Südhoff draws on the German HDP Community of Practice and the view of Grand Bargain Ambassador Michael Köhler — who described the nexus landscape as still dominated by a 'Community of Theory' — to argue that rigorous, context-specific criteria must guide nexus ambitions. Timely given the USAID collapse and German humanitarian strategy shifts.

Title: Mind the gap! UNHCR, humanitarian assistance and the development process
Abstract:
This paper assesses UNHCR's evolving role in bridging humanitarian assistance and development. It reviews historical approaches from the refugee aid and development initiatives of the 1970s-80s, which aimed at promoting self-sufficiency and sustainable development in refugee-hosting areas, to the 'returnee aid and development' strategy of the 1990s, focused on reintegration of repatriated populations.

The paper highlights challenges such as the funding gaps, the unclear objectives of development strategies, and difficulties in inter-agency coordination. It explores the Brookings process initiated in the late 1990s to address post-conflict reconstruction.

Critiques assert the need for UNHCR to avoid overextension into development tasks, suggesting instead that it should focus on its core strengths in protection and immediate assistance while collaborating with development agencies. Future efforts may benefit from considering the developmental impact on refugee-hosting areas alongside repatriation strategies.

Title: Moving Beyond the Emergency: A Whole of Society Approach to the Refugee Response in Bangladesh
Abstract:
The document discusses the necessity of a medium-term response plan for the Rohingya refugee crisis in Bangladesh, particularly in Cox's Bazar. Bangladesh hosts over one million Rohingya refugees, and the crisis is increasingly protracted with no immediate prospect of repatriation.

The document highlights inefficiencies of the current short-term humanitarian response, focusing solely on basic aid without addressing complex needs such as food security, health, and social cohesion. It recommends a 'whole of society' approach to improve outcomes for both refugees and host communities by enhancing self-reliance through access to work and education. Challenges include restrictive policies and inadequate financing.

The document advocates for an inclusive plan coordinated by stakeholders, supported by multiyear financing and policy reforms to strengthen local infrastructure and improve economic opportunities, aimed at building long-term sustainable outcomes for all affected populations.

Title: OECD DAC INCAF Common Position on Addressing Forced Displacement with a Comprehensive Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus Approach
Abstract:
Common position adopted in November 2023 by the OECD Development Assistance Committee's International Network on Conflict and Fragility (INCAF), contextualising the 2019 DAC Recommendation on the HDP Nexus specifically for forced displacement situations. 

Announced as a multi-stakeholder pledge to the Global Compact on Refugees at the 2023 Global Refugee Forum, it sets out three engagement areas for development cooperation in refugee, internal displacement and statelessness situations in low- and middle-income countries: (1) early engagement of development, peace and climate action alongside humanitarian aid in new displacement situations; (2) inclusion of displaced persons and stateless people in national development plans and systems; and (3) comprehensive finance to support affected host countries. Reaffirms that the 2019 DAC Recommendation always requires peace and conflict-sensitive approaches, and development approaches wherever possible, in forced displacement contexts.

Abstract:

Drawing on field experience and NGO perspectives, it analyses how humanitarian, development and peace actors have navigated the collapse of state institutions, severe access restrictions, and the securitisation of aid under military rule.

Title: Operationalizing Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development (PCRD) in Africa: Integrating Displacement within Peacebuilding Efforts
Abstract:

Title: Operationalizing the HDP Nexus in WFP Western Africa. Case Study: Chad
Abstract:
This WFP case study presents findings from a 2023-2024 learning exercise by WFP's Regional Bureau in Dakar to identify HDP nexus emergent and good practices in Chad. Chad represents one of the most complex and protracted humanitarian contexts in West Africa, combining conflict-driven displacement, climate shocks, chronic food insecurity, and the regional Lake Chad Basin crisis.

The case study examines how WFP has navigated nexus programming in this environment, including how it coordinates with development and peace actors, how it sequences humanitarian and resilience activities, and what operational lessons can be drawn for future nexus design. It feeds into WFP's broader evidence-building programme on nexus approaches in Western Africa and provides country-specific insights complementary to the general WFP HDP Nexus Case Studies series.

Title: Operationalizing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Iraq
Abstract:
This UNDP country case study examines how the HDP Nexus functioned primarily as a transition mechanism in Iraq, helping shift from humanitarian response toward government-led development and peace efforts following the defeat of ISIL.

UNDP was central to this transition through its Funding Facility for Stabilization (FFS), which completed over 3,700 projects worth over USD 1 billion, creating conditions for nearly 5 million displaced Iraqis to return home. The Social Cohesion Programme supported IDP reintegration through community dialogue, dispute resolution, and livelihood support, mediating over 500 disputes. UNDP co-led the Durable Solutions Task Force with IOM and the Durable Solutions Technical Working Group.

Key lessons highlight that stabilization is essential for enabling development, that the Durable Solutions architecture is effective for HDP coordination, and that overcoming siloed financing is critical to unlocking the Nexus potential in the context of shrinking humanitarian funding.

Title: Operationalizing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Ukraine
Abstract:
This UNDP country case study analyses the evolution of the HDP Nexus in Ukraine from 2014 through 2024, shaped by Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. 

Ukraine represents a unique context where national and local authorities remained functional during active conflict, enabling early investment in recovery. UNDP championed the Nexus through co-leading the Durable Solutions Working Group with IOM and UNHCR, developing large-scale joint assessments including the Human Impact Assessment and Social Cohesion and Reconciliation Index (SCORE), and delivering recovery programming through the UN Recovery and Peacebuilding Programme, the EU4Recovery initiative, and the R4 (Reconstruction, Returns, Recovery and Reform) framework. The Green Energy Recovery Programme restored energy access for 6 million people.

Key lessons highlight that HDP coordination gains traction during active conflict when state institutions remain functional, and that without aligned financing, shared metrics, and sustained coordination, even well-resourced contexts risk fragmented responses.

Title: Operationalizing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Yemen
Abstract: This UNDP country case study examines the operationalization of the HDP Nexus in Yemen from 2016 to 2024, a country facing severe protracted crisis marked by active conflict, large-scale displacement, institutional collapse, and widespread food insecurity. The case demonstrates how UNDP acted as a central convener, thought leader, and implementer, establishing HDP coordination platforms including the Yemen Partner Group and Yemen Partner Technical Team, co-chairing the Food Security and Livelihoods Working Group with FAO and the World Bank, and leading area-based pilots in Taiz and Lahj governorates. Key programmatic entry points include the EU-funded Enhanced Rural Resilience in Yemen (ERRY) programme supporting over 2.1 million Yemenis and the Peace Support Facility supporting mediation and social cohesion. Key lessons highlight the importance of adaptable strategies, community-led approaches, flexible Nexus-supportive financing, deliberate investment in the peace component, and gender-sensitive programming.

Title: Operationalizing The Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus Lessons From Colombia, Mali, Nigeria, Somalia And Turkey
Abstract:
The report by the International Organization for Migration examines the operationalization of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDPN) in Colombia, Mali, Nigeria, Somalia, and Turkey. It highlights the necessity of integrated efforts between humanitarian, development, and peace actions to address complex protracted crises exacerbated by displacement, conflict, and disasters. It underscores the importance of national legal frameworks and dedicated laws in countries to build capacity for sustained crisis responses.

Key lessons include the role of peace agreements, coherent donor policies, effective coordination structures, and multi-year funding strategies as enablers of successful HDPN implementation. The report suggests that HDPN leaders need multidisciplinary acumen and political skills to navigate challenges and proposes strategic planning processes for HDPN actors, emphasizing flexible financing, better coordination, and exit strategies aligned with governance indicators.

Title: Opportunities, Challenges and Approaches to Implementing the HDP Nexus at Country Level
Abstract:
In Autumn 2023, the Centre for International Peace Operations (ZIF) organized a workshop series focusing on the implementation of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus at the country level.

The series aimed to facilitate the exchange of experiences among German organizations involved in humanitarian aid, development cooperation, and peace work. Key topics included coordination, localisation, peacebuilding, and financing within the HDP nexus. Participants developed concrete recommendations for operationalizing the nexus, addressed to relevant ministries like the GFFO and BMZ. These recommendations emphasized enhanced coordination between national and international actors, the role of local structures in peace efforts, improved funding mechanisms, and the need for flexibility and adaptability in crisis responses.

The report highlights the benefits of collective and collaborative approaches to addressing protracted crises and suggests the establishment of an ongoing community of practice. Challenges such as implementation constraints at the local level and the alignment of funding pools were also discussed, emphasizing the need for further dialogue and strategic engagement among stakeholders.

Title: Paradigm shift: the Humanitarian Development Nexus in Cox's Bazar District, Bangladesh
Abstract:
The case study explores the humanitarian-development nexus in the Cox's Bazar District of Bangladesh, focusing on challenges in Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH). Cox's Bazar is marked by low human development indicators, frequent natural disasters, and pressures from the Rohingya refugee crisis, exacerbating the district's vulnerabilities. UNICEF has implemented multi-dimensional strategies involving WASH improvement, emergency response, community engagement in sanitation practices, and women's leadership to enhance the living conditions and resilience of the host and internally displaced communities.

Key initiatives include promoting blended emergency and development programs, establishing Open Defecation-Free communities, and ensuring access to safe water and sanitation during emergencies. Despite progress, significant WASH gaps remain. The study highlights lessons learned, such as the importance of community mobilization and women\'s leadership, and suggests a need for research on disaster-resilient WASH practices to support future planning and advocacy efforts.

Title: Pathways for Peace: Inclusive Approaches to Preventing Violent Conflict
Abstract: This landmark joint United Nations and World Bank report makes the case for a fundamental refocusing of the international community's attention on conflict prevention. Based on a review of cases where prevention has been successful, it argues that a scaled-up system for preventive action would save between US$5 billion and $70 billion per year. The report stresses the centrality of inclusion — from access to power, natural resources, security and justice — as the root of many violent conflicts, and recommends that development processes better interact with diplomacy, mediation, and security tools. It calls for a coherent, whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach that bridges humanitarian, development, and peace action to prevent conflicts from becoming violent.

Title: Personal attitudes of individuals working in the fields of humanitarian, development and peace regarding the HDP Nexus
Abstract:
This thesis by Marina Muenchenbach explores the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus, detailing personal attitudes of individuals working in these fields. Through interviews with 38 professionals, the study identifies positive and negative attitudes towards the nexus, alongside operational challenges and conceptual dilemmas. Major findings include concerns about institutional resistance, conceptual vagueness, and feasibility issues, as well as the political challenges in implementing the nexus effectively. 

The thesis discusses the potential of the HDP Nexus for more holistic approaches by bridging humanitarian aid, development, and peacebuilding, although practical examples of peace work remain sparse. Recommendations include reworking the overall approach to clearly define peace elements, addressing dilemmas from different mandates, and enhancing coordination among relevant parties. Proposed operational improvements focus on better implementation modalities, financing strategies, and local stakeholder engagement to foster a sustainable and coordinated inter-agency response to crises.

Title: Preparedness Enablers' Guide
Abstract:
The Preparedness Enablers' Guide (PEG) offers a comprehensive framework for enhancing disaster preparedness through a systems-strengthening approach.

The guide is developed by the Global Logistics Cluster as part of the Field Based Preparedness Project (FBPP) and aims to advance sustainable localization by empowering local actors. It emphasizes the importance of understanding complex adaptive systems, investing in change management skills, and prioritizing localization strategies.

The guide critiques traditional capacity development methodologies, highlighting challenges such as terminological ambiguity, implementation failures, and dependency traps like isomorphic mimicry. Alternatives include recentering capacity development efforts around local actors, addressing different capacity types and levels, and focusing on institutionalization. Tools such as stakeholder mapping, and ability and readiness indexing are suggested for comprehensive context analysis and capacity assessments.

The guide concludes by outlining steps for designing, implementing, and monitoring capacity development engagements with an emphasis on sustainability and mutual learning.

Abstract:

Title: Programming Considerations for Humanitarian-Development-Peace Coherence: A Note for USAID's Implementing Partners
Abstract:
The practical note by USAID\'s Resilience Leadership Council elaborates on Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) coherence, aiming to enhance collaboration among humanitarian, development, and peace actors for a common agenda, maximizing impact and sustainability of programs. It highlights USAID\'s commitment to HDP principles, including upholding humanitarian principles, planning jointly, integrating conflict sensitivity, and strengthening local systems.

Title: Programming Guide: Conflict Sensitivity and Peacebuilding
Abstract:
The Programming Guide: Conflict Sensitivity and Peacebuilding by UNICEF provides field staff and leadership with guidance on integrating conflict sensitivity and peacebuilding into their programs. It emphasizes that conflict significantly impacts UNICEF's efforts and conversely, UNICEF's interventions can influence conflict dynamics. The guide promotes a systematic approach to conflict-sensitive programming to mitigate negative impacts, and peacebuilding programming to positively address root causes of conflict.

Key components include conflict analysis, program design, theories of change, and monitoring and evaluation systems. Furthermore, the guide outlines how to integrate these approaches at policy, community, and individual levels, highlighting the roles of social services sectors like education, health, and WASH in fostering social cohesion. The flexibility of the guide allows its application across different contexts, aiming to enhance capacities for transitioning out of fragility, reducing violent relapses, and achieving sustainable results for children.

Title: Protection and the Humanitarian-Development Nexus: A Literature Review
Abstract:
This literature review from the Local Engagement Refugee Research Network (LERRN) examines the intersection of protection programming and the humanitarian-development nexus. It synthesises academic and policy literature on how protection concerns — including refugee protection, child protection, gender-based violence, and human rights — relate to and should be integrated into nexus approaches.

The review identifies key tensions between the immediate, principled nature of protection work and the longer-term, more politically engaged development approaches required by the nexus, and examines how different actors have navigated these tensions in practice across multiple country contexts.

Title: Protection and the nexus: tensions and opportunities
Abstract:
The report discusses the humanitarian-development nexus, particularly its implications for protection actors. It emphasizes the importance of a coordinated approach across humanitarian and development assistance to address protracted crises effectively. The nexus approach advocates for collective outcomes, which involve comprehensive planning and collaboration between various stakeholders to ensure both immediate aid and long-term development goals are met.

The report identifies opportunities for protection actors in the nexus, such as durable solutions for displacement, building state social systems for protection services, and strengthening justice, rule of law, and accountability. It also highlights the challenges and risks, including potential threats to humanitarian principles, the need for state accountability, and the limits of humanitarian actors' mandates. 

Recommendations include establishing workstreams on the nexus approach, enhancing strategic planning, and ensuring proper coordination mechanisms to foster collaboration between humanitarians and development actors.

Title: Qatar's Approach across the Triple Nexus in Conflict-Affected Contexts: The Case of Darfur
Abstract:
The purpose of this paper is to document Qatar’s recent contribution of humanitarian, development, and peace-related efforts to the Sudanese in Darfur. It delves deeply into Qatar’s involvement in Darfur by tracing the flow of foreign assistance provided between 2011 and 2018, while analysing the relevant mediation efforts to settle the conflict in the region. 

The paper calls for adopting the Triple Nexus approach – or humanitarian development-peace nexus in dealing with Qatar’s role as a third party in Darfur both as a donor and mediator. Contextualising Qatar’s role in this context necessitates considering its foreign assistance and peace-related efforts in conflict-affected contexts and its positioning in relation to the Triple Nexus. While Qatar has not publicly committed itself to the Triple Nexus reforms directed to OECD-DAC donor countries, the paper argues that adopting the Triple Nexus approach might develop the prevailing humanitarian and development and peace-related assistance practices in Qatar.

Title: Ready to Change? Building flexibility into the triple nexus
Abstract:
This report explores the importance of flexibility in implementing the humanitarian-development-peace nexus (triple nexus) in fragile and protracted crises. It argues that in these settings, crisis-affected populations require responses that address both immediate and long-term needs concurrently, rather than sequentially. Nexus programming must overcome the rigidity typical of humanitarian or development approaches by being context-driven and focusing on evolving local dynamics. 

The study features case studies from Christian Aid, World Vision, and the Norwegian Refugee Council in countries like Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and Cameroon. These organizations piloted flexible programming approaches that included anticipatory strategies based on scenario planning and adaptive strategies using community feedback. Challenges such as funding inflexibility, procurement delays, and a lack of adaptive management systems were identified as barriers to effective nexus programming.

The report concludes that embedding flexibility into agency operations is critical to adapting to the complex needs of populations in crisis settings and transforming nexus concepts into impactful practice.

Title: Realities and Myths of the "Triple Nexus" Local Perspectives on Peacebuilding, Development, and Humanitarian Action in Mali
Abstract:
This journal article analyzes the challenges faced by Mali, a country destabilized by poverty, violence, and political instability. Despite being labeled a 'model democracy' and receiving significant international aid, Mali suffers from ongoing inter-ethnic tensions and weakened governance structures. The paper explores key factors contributing to the instability: Tuareg separatism, stultified state-building, and the spread of conservative Islamic and jihadist influences.

The international response, including interventions by foreign troops and peacebuilding initiatives, is scrutinized for its effectiveness. The paper questions the applicability of the 'triple nexus' approach, which attempts to align humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding efforts, and critiques the blurred boundaries between these operations. Interviews reveal deep skepticism about the nexus's potential to improve the situation in Mali, highlighting concerns about the possible politicization of humanitarian actions and the lack of local inclusivity.

Ultimately, the article calls for rethinking strategies to empower local communities while addressing the systemic failures in governance and peacebuilding efforts.

Title: Recovery and Peacebuilding Assessment Toolkit
Abstract:
The Recovery and Peacebuilding Assessment (RPBA) Toolkit provides guidance for teams conducting joint recovery and peacebuilding assessments in countries transitioning out of conflict or political crisis. A joint methodology developed by the United Nations, the World Bank, and the European Union, the RPBA aims to ensure that international and national interventions for recovery are aligned by helping countries assess, plan and prioritize requirements under a common process.

The toolkit includes a practical note on assessment and planning, guidance on prioritization and costing, and sector-specific tools. The RPBA has been applied in contexts including the Central African Republic, North-East Nigeria, Mali, Ukraine and others, providing an evidence-based assessment of recovery and peacebuilding requirements as a platform for consensus building.

Title: Réflexion: éléments tirés des évaluations: la localisation des ODD par la gouvernance
Abstract:
This document presents lessons learned from initiatives conducted by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and other agencies in localizing Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) via local governance. Successful localization of SDGs requires coordination across governance levels and stakeholder engagement, including varied viewpoints and recognizing marginalized communities. 

The UNDP's initiatives proved effective in several countries, strengthening local governments\' capacity, transparency, accountability, and harnessing local data for planning. Programs targeting local SDG integration faced challenges, such as coordination issues and insufficient capacity building, but produced notable successes in countries like India, Nepal, Cuba, Malawi, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Stakeholder inclusion and structured engagement are essential for fostering local ownership of SDG initiatives.

The use of voluntary local reviews offers a promising approach to accelerate local SDG progress by aligning national priorities with local needs and enhancing transparency. Despite some challenges, these initiatives underscore the importance of tailored, continuous support for effective SDG localization.

Title: Reframing Displacement Crises as Development Opportunities
Abstract:
The policy paper 'Reframing Displacement Crises as Development Opportunities' explores the potential of viewing displacement not only as a humanitarian challenge but also as an opportunity for development. It argues that large-scale displacements, such as refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs), present impacts and opportunities beyond humanitarian needs, affecting human capital, economic growth, and host communities.

The paper promotes a development-led approach that integrates displaced populations into economic systems by leveraging their skills and resources, engaging the private sector, and implementing market-led strategies. It emphasizes the need to harmonize humanitarian and development efforts by mainstreaming displaced populations into development planning and improving fiscal responses to the economic challenges posed by displaced populations.

The policy note advocates for a proactive role for governments and donors to optimize economic contributions from displaced populations and reduce negative impacts, leading to sustainable socio-economic benefits for both refugees and host communities.

Title: Relief, Recovery and Resilience: World Vision HDP Nexus Programming in Northern Bahr el Ghazal, South Sudan
Abstract: This World Vision Germany study examines project-level HDP nexus implementation and coordination in Northern Bahr el Ghazal, South Sudan — a region facing mutually reinforcing shocks including conflict, flooding, and chronic underdevelopment. Commissioned by World Vision Germany, the study focuses on two linked projects delivered under the German Chapeau framework, assessing how effectively they were coordinated within and across the nexus, what complementarities and gaps emerged, and what transferable lessons can be drawn for future nexus design. Key findings suggest that aligning humanitarian and development efforts is possible in fragile, flood-prone areas when there is strong field coordination, flexible management, and locally embedded teams. The study contributes empirically-grounded insights to the broader HDP nexus discourse and aims to refine World Vision Germany's next generation of programming.

Title: Resilience and Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
Abstract:

For ECHO, resilience — understood as the capacity of households, communities, and systems to withstand, adapt to, and recover from shocks — is both a core objective and a key bridge between the humanitarian and development pillars of the nexus.

The document explains how the EU integrates resilience considerations into its nexus programming, covering how resilience analysis informs joint situation assessment, how resilience-oriented programming can address both immediate vulnerability and structural drivers of crisis, and how the EU's financing instruments — including ECHO humanitarian financing and DEVCO development cooperation instruments — can be aligned to support multi-year resilience investments across the nexus. The resolution calls for more coherent, integrated and inclusive approaches to preventing conflict and sustaining peace, emphasising that humanitarian, development and peacebuilding dimensions of action must be mutually reinforcing. It is foundational for the peace pillar of the HDP Nexus, calling on the UN system to work collectively to address the root causes of conflict, support national and local actors, and ensure that development strategies are underpinned by conflict sensitivity and the goal of sustaining peace.

The article recognizes the challenges of integrating peacebuilding within the triple-nexus, such as maintaining impartiality, engaging with state actors, and managing conflicting priorities. Overall, the authors recommend more localized, integrative, and context-sensitive approaches to increase resilience and effectively operationalize the nexus in chronic conflict zones.

The EiE field has been at the forefront of nexus thinking in the education sector, recognising that immediate crisis education response must be designed to strengthen — rather than replace or undermine — national education systems, and that quality inclusive education is itself a contribution to social cohesion and peacebuilding.

The toolkit covers the key principles of inclusive quality EiE, including how to conduct inclusive needs assessments, how to adapt educational content to conflict and crisis contexts, how to work with national systems and local actors, how to mainstream gender, disability, and conflict sensitivity, and how to plan for the transition from emergency response to sustainable educational recovery.
