Title: Unveiling Challenges and Gaps in Climate Finance in Conflict Areas
Abstract:
This SIPRI Insights paper (October 2024) addresses the critical mismatch between climate finance allocation and vulnerability in conflict-affected countries. Drawing on OECD CRS data and Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative vulnerability scores, the authors find that conflict-affected countries — which are among the most climate-vulnerable globally — consistently receive insufficient climate adaptation finance relative to their needs. Conflict exacerbates populations' vulnerability to climate change by undermining adaptive capacity, worsening food insecurity, and deepening inequalities, yet active conflict zones remain dramatically underserved by climate finance mechanisms.

The paper examines institutional barriers — risk aversion by climate funds, inability to programme in insecure areas, and design of climate mechanisms around stable governance contexts — and calls for systemic changes to deliver climate finance through HDP nexus-compatible instruments. Abstract:

The document outlines ten principles that guide the project management cycle, from assessment and design to implementation and evaluation.

Key principles include focusing on locality, collaborating across sectors, adaptive management, and ensuring that actions are people-centered and utilize existing structures. The document advocates for flexible programming and emphasizes the importance of planning for scalability. Title: WASH Triple Nexus: Building resilience and sustainability in fragile and disaster-prone contexts

The event report summarizes a webinar focused on the Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) Triple Nexus approach, which integrates humanitarian, development, and peace efforts. The webinar hosted by SWA highlighted the importance of resilience and sustainability in fragile and disaster-prone contexts.

Key speakers, including Jeff Goldberg from USAID and Tim Grieve, emphasized collaboration across various sectors and stakeholders. Successful case studies were shared, such as Uganda's integration of refugee water needs and Honduras' targeted emergency response to typhoons. Title: WE Nexus: Empowered Women for sustainable peace: Addressing peace-humanitarian Nexus to enhance community resilience in Indonesia
Abstract:
The brief outlines the 'Empowered Women for Sustainable Peace' project in Indonesia, focusing on the humanitarian-development-peace nexus to enhance community resilience. It addresses Indonesia's challenges such as conflicts, natural hazards, displacement, gender inequality, and radicalization. The project aims to empower women and girls by expanding their roles in conflict prevention, resolution, and recovery, promoting a gender-sensitive approach across national and local governance, disaster risk reduction, and economic resilience.

Key strategies include increasing women's participation in village forums and policies, strengthening multi-stakeholder platforms for collaboration, and implementing gender-responsive solutions at the community level. The project leverages the Women, Peace and Security Agenda and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction to explore scalable interventions, contributing to a peaceful and just society while concurrently addressing immediate humanitarian needs and promoting sustainable development and peace-building efforts.

Title: Weathering Change: Exploring Connections between Climate Adaptation and Conflict Prevention in Mali
Abstract:
This Mercy Corps research report (published January 2025 as version 3.0) examines the connections between climate adaptation and conflict prevention in Mali, one of the world's most fragile and climate-vulnerable countries. Based on the Ben ni Baara programme — which integrated conflict management, economic resilience, and community-state relationship strengthening — the report analyses how climate stressors (particularly drought and the timing of rainy seasons) interact with intercommunal conflict between farmers and herders.

The report explores how Mercy Corps' Climate-Conflict Assessment methodology identifies entry points to interrupt the cycle of fragility, and what programme design choices can simultaneously address climate change drivers and conflict risk factors. Mali is identified as particularly difficult for nexus implementation given the security vacuum following the exit of international military missions; findings offer lessons for programming in similarly constrained contexts.

Title: Weathering the Storm: Why and How Development Financing Actors Should Stay Engaged During Political Crises
Abstract: This NRC research report (May 2024) examines the humanitarian consequences when development aid is suspended following unconstitutional changes of government (UCG), drawing on case studies from Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Afghanistan. It finds that while donors maintain humanitarian funding post-UCG, withdrawal of development finance forces humanitarian actors to fill gaps in basic services, exacerbating the funding crisis and undermining the nexus approach. The report directly addresses the tension between principled donor conditionality and the DAC Recommendation on the HDP nexus, arguing for pragmatic mechanisms to maintain development engagement even in politically constrained environments. A timely contribution given the post-2025 aid funding crisis and the collapse of USAID.

Title: West and Central Africa Regional Policy Dialogue The New Way of Working: from delivering aid to ending need
Abstract:
The West and Central Africa Regional Policy Dialogue report outlines the importance of integrating humanitarian and development efforts, as discussed at a workshop in Dakar. This approach, termed the 'New Way of Working', aims to achieve collective outcomes, anticipate crises, and strengthen local systems, aligning with Sustainable Development Goals. Significant challenges include improving data analysis, joint planning across sectors, coordinating efforts, and securing multi-year financing. 

Key recommendations advocate for aligning short-term and long-term planning processes, integrating national and local capacities, and improving trust in data sharing. The event showcased steps already underway in several African countries, emphasizing collaboration between diverse actors including governments, NGOs, and international organizations to deliver on collective outcomes, focusing on risk reduction and vulnerability mitigation.

Title: WFP Conflict Sensitivity Mainstreaming Strategy
Abstract:
The WFP Conflict Sensitivity Mainstreaming Strategy emphasizes the importance of adopting a conflict-sensitive approach in all operational settings to mitigate potential risks and enhance program effectiveness. Recognizing conflict as a major driver of food insecurity, the strategy outlines a comprehensive framework to integrate conflict sensitivity into WFP's program cycle, emphasizing assessment, strategic planning, and implementation. It highlights the critical roles of conflict analysis and risk assessments in identifying interaction with local contexts. WFP commits to building capacities at various organizational levels and establishing partnerships to enhance context understandings and document risks systematically.

The strategy advocates for cultural and institutional shifts, detailing responsibilities across functional areas to ensure that operations do not exacerbate existing tensions. It explores issues regarding cooperation with partner agencies, vendor selection, and relations with host and donor governments, while underscoring the need for targeted workforce planning, capacity building, and specialized training efforts.

The strategy aims to align with the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus and promote accountability by incorporating conflict sensitivity into its programming processes across diverse operational landscapes.

Title: WFP Peace Measurement Roundtable: Compendium of Reference Group Presentations
Abstract:
The WFP Peace Measurement Roundtable serves as a forum discussing different approaches and methodologies to contribute and measure peace. It reflects on strategies like conflict sensitivity and resilience-building from organizations like Sida, BMZ, JICA, and others, aiming to enhance peace through transparent and inclusive institutions, dialogue, and mediation processes.

The document highlights the value of monitoring impacts on conflict and peace, affirming the need for systematic tools and strategies that leverage local capacities while being mindful of unintended negative effects. Peace measurements and engagement strategies are explored in various contexts, including countries like Bangladesh and the Philippines, where diverse factors such as social cohesion and risk analysis are considered vital for operational success in complex environments. 

Collaboration between partners and adaptive management is emphasized to foster resilience and improve peacebuilding outcomes while ensuring accountability and effectiveness across interventions.

Title: What Can We Learn? Case Studies on the Triple Nexus in West Africa
Abstract:
This Oxfam case study collection (June 2023) examines how Oxfam's interventions in West Africa are adapting to the triple nexus approach, which challenges the linear and sequential logic of traditional aid delivery. The collection argues that humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding programmes must operate simultaneously to address systemic inequalities that keep people vulnerable — requiring fundamental transformations in how both humanitarian and development sectors work. 

Case studies span Oxfam programmes in countries across West Africa, illustrating how nexus thinking is being put into practice at programme level. The collection offers practical lessons for multi-mandate organisations navigating the tension between principled humanitarian action and the demands of integrated, longer-term programming in conflict-affected and climate-stressed contexts.

Title: What Does 'Sustaining Peace' Mean? Guidance Note
Abstract:
This UN Peacebuilding Support Office guidance note provides an accessible explanation of the 'sustaining peace' concept endorsed by the 2016 UN General Assembly and Security Council resolutions. It explains what sustaining peace means as an overarching goal for the UN system, how it relates to and differs from earlier approaches to peacebuilding, and what it implies for different types of UN actors.

The guidance clarifies how sustaining peace connects to the HDP nexus, the 2030 Agenda, and humanitarian action, and provides practical guidance on how resident coordinators, UN country teams, and other actors can operationalise the sustaining peace agenda in their work.

Title: Who Decides on Humanitarian Reform? Local Actors and the Nexus
Abstract: This ODI insight piece (August 2025) from the Humanitarian Policy Group documents perspectives from local humanitarian actors in Yemen, Colombia, and Myanmar on the ongoing 'humanitarian reset' and what systemic reform must look like from their vantage point. It directly addresses the structural obstacles that local actors face in engaging with the HDP nexus: the technical challenge of coordinating between donors with separate humanitarian and development offices; the structural problem of silos preventing holistic assessment of community needs; and the exclusion of local actors from decision-making that results in programming misaligned with community priorities. The piece argues for new coordination models — with local actors leading on design and delivery, and INGOs and UN agencies serving as technical and financial oversight intermediaries — and places the nexus reform agenda squarely in the context of localisation and accountability to affected populations.

Title: Whose Nexus? When the System Lags Behind Frontline Actors: The Case of the Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) in Sudan
Abstract: Blog post in NORRAG's HDP Nexus blog series, developed from a contribution to the NORRAG Policy Insights collection Education and the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus at 10. Using the case of Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) — the grassroots mutual aid networks awarded the 2025 Chatham House Prize — the authors challenge international donors and agencies to follow the lead of local actors who are already operationalising the nexus from the bottom up, including on education. Argues that when formal international systems lag behind frontline actors, the nexus risks becoming a top-down framework that fails to recognise, resource or learn from locally-driven solutions. A pointed critique of the gap between nexus rhetoric and the realities facing local actors in active conflict settings.

Title: WHS High-Level Anniversary event: Advancing the New Way of Working
Abstract:
The WHS High-Level Anniversary event held in Istanbul in May 2017 focused on advancing the New Way of Working (NWOW), which aims to integrate humanitarian, development, and peace efforts from the onset of crises. The event emphasized the necessity of collaboration across sectors to transcend traditional divides and pursue collective outcomes, particularly in protracted crises. Participants highlighted obstacles such as coordination issues, lack of flexible financing, and the need for structural change to support long-term activities.

Recommendations included strengthening field-level leadership, aligning planning processes, and engaging multi-stakeholder collaboration including governments, NGOs, and private sectors. The NWOW is seen as a critical strategy for accelerating the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) achievement, providing a coherent roadmap to reduce risks and vulnerabilities while facilitating sustainable development and peacebuilding.

Discussions highlighted examples from countries like Nigeria, Ethiopia, and CAR, demonstrating how NWOW principles can be operationalized in diverse contexts to better address crises and support affected communities.

Title: Women, Land and Peace Key Messages
Abstract:
The report titled 'Women, Land and Peace Key Messages' highlights the critical role of women in achieving sustainable peace through empowering them with access to land rights and ownership in fragile and conflict-affected situations. It emphasizes the importance of securing women\'s land rights in such contexts as essential for their protection, empowerment, and participation in peacebuilding.

The document underscores the significance of inclusive and participatory approaches to land governance, which ensure women's rights and combat vulnerabilities stemming from conflict. It calls for the integration of gender-sensitive land rights into national and international strategies to foster stability and peace, and stresses the need for effective implementation mechanisms.

The report identifies key areas for action, such as strengthening women's capacity to claim land rights, facilitating legal access, and overcoming barriers posed by traditional and systemic discrimination.

Abstract:

Title: Working across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus: What can we learn from evaluations?
Abstract:
This evaluation, authored by Lezlie Morinière and Susanna Morrison-Métois, assesses the implementation of the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus across various organizations. The study, based on 90 evaluations, reveals a broad spectrum of approaches and understanding of the nexus. It highlights structural challenges such as fragmented funding and coordination mechanisms, the integration of peace with humanitarian and development efforts, and the role of various actors from government to civil society and the private sector.

The analysis underscores the need for strengthened capacities, localized approaches, and greater focus on climate and conflict-sensitive programming. Despite progress in some areas, deep systemic issues in international aid architecture, including siloed funding and inadequate coordination frameworks, hamper the effectiveness of nexus approaches.

The paper calls for improved implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of nexus approaches to genuinely benefit affected populations, enhance collective outcomes, and ensure sustainable peace and development.

Title: Workshop on the Humanitarian Development Peace Nexus in Ukraine (English)
Abstract:
This OCHA event report documents a workshop held in June 2021 on the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Ukraine, bringing together humanitarian and development actors to discuss how the nexus approach can be applied in the Ukrainian context.

The workshop examined the opportunities and challenges for advancing HDP coherence in Ukraine — a country experiencing conflict in the east while simultaneously pursuing development and European integration. It covered coordination mechanisms, joint programming, financing approaches, and the specific dynamics of applying the nexus in a context where the state retains significant capacity. Title: Yemen and the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Triple Nexus: Analytical Paper
Abstract:
This analytical paper (May 2024, No. 6), produced by the Yemeni Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation (MOPIC), assesses the HDP nexus approach from a national government perspective in Yemen — one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. It examines the theoretical foundations of the nexus, performance of HDP coordination mechanisms in Yemen's split governance context (Government of Yemen/Ansar Allah), and the challenge of reinstating national development institutions in a context where international actors have come to dominate humanitarian and development programming.

The paper calls for a shift from emergency response to resilience-building and for stronger complementarity and partnership between the donor community, international organisations, and national structures. A rare government-authored national nexus assessment, available in Arabic and English.

Title: Yemen National Guidelines: Scaling up Sustainable Multisectoral Nutrition Investments and Interventions
Abstract:
This document presents Yemen's national guidelines for scaling up sustainable multisectoral nutrition investments and interventions, developed in the context of the country's protracted humanitarian crisis and with a view to applying HDP Nexus principles to nutrition programming. 

The guidelines address the challenge of moving beyond emergency treatment of acute malnutrition towards prevention-oriented, development-aligned approaches that can address the structural drivers of malnutrition in Yemen. They outline coordination mechanisms between humanitarian and development nutrition actors, financing frameworks that link humanitarian funding with longer-term investments, and programmatic approaches that involve government systems, local capacities and community-based interventions.
